six years of privileged living; elementary school chess champion, prep
school valedictorian, Ivy League graduate and member of countless
exclusive clubs and teams, but never before had he wanted a title as badly

Like a school boy with a crush, Robert began to scribble the word
"shipowner" on a piece of paper when he got back to his desk, but he
quickly hesitated. He didn't know if ‘shipowner' was one word or two so
instead he wrote, "Robert Fairchild - Shipping Man."
As luck would have it, in just four months he would be returning to
Harvard for his 20th Reunion and would do whatever was necessary to own
a ship by then.

monasteries, and mining its teachings for affirmation of the legitimacy of
his own rule.

title: Commerce
summary:
Archaeological and written records testify to the diversity of routes and
goods in circulation around the Mediterranean, yet in the late Roman period
a preponderance of shipping was dedicated to the annona, shipments of
grain to be made into bread for free distribution to the masses-the bread of
"bread and circuses." This practice underwent drastic change in the fourth
century when the Alexandrian fleets were redirected to Constantinople and
those of Africa declined in significance as the population of Rome
dwindled. In the sixth century, an estimated twelve hundred to eighteen
hundred ships were involved in the annona trade, most of them making two
round-trips in a season.

title: Christopher Columbus
summary:
The exploratory activity on the Atlantic had attracted any number of
ambitious mariners, one of whom, the Genoese-born Christopher
Columbus, conceived a bold plan "that he would sail south and west,
discovering great stretches of highly fertile land, both islands and terra
firma, all extremely rich in gold and silver, pearls and precious stones and
teeming peoples; and that, sailing in this direction, he would eventually
come to the land of India, with the noble island of Cipangu [Japan] and the
realms of the Grand Khan." He was not the first to believe such a voyage
was possible, and one can say with complete candor that he failed:
Columbus underestimated the size of the earth; he did not reach Asia; and
he did not tap into the great spiceries of the Orient. None of this diminishes
his epochal accomplishment in establishing an unbroken link between
Eurasia and Africa in the east and the Americas in the west.

title: Capesize
summary: A slight rally earlier in the week with an increase in transatlantic and fronthaul cargoes highlighting a tightening of North Atlantic tonnage. A 180,000-tonner fixed for a transatlantic round at $11,000 daily and 170,000 tonner went at $9,000 daily but since then rates have eased.

title: Panamax
summary: The Atlantic focus remained on fronthaul cargoes with fixing from the US Gulf and east coast South America to the East although the latter continued to be serviced by ships coming from the Indian Ocean area and further afield. Rates in both areas hovered around the mid $12,000 daily plus mid $200,000 bonus with some higher and slightly lower rates agreed depending on the specification of the ships.

title: Supramax
summary: Those looking for a floor to the supramax market this week were left disappointed as tonnage lists continued to lengthen in most areas. Charterers were able to pick and choose in the South Atlantic where it was reported that a 2006 Japanese built 53,500 dwt vessel was booked for a trip from Recalada to Singapore-Japan at $10,500 daily plus a ballast of $100,000.

title: Capesize
summary: Yet another depressing week for capesizes with rates slipping again in the East and in the Atlantic. Too many ships in the East continued to weigh on the market and although some of the majors have been taking ships for West Australia, each has been at successively lower rates.

title: Panamax
summary: Fronthaul business fixed with no ballast bonuses from the US Gulf to the East shocked the market this week. There were mitigating circumstances - early committed ships needing to go east and in one instance for drydock.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Another very tough week for the owners as the market in all areas continued to crumble. Activity was limited in the US Gulf although a nice 61,400 dwt 2011 built ‘ultra' type open US Atlantic was paid a relatively encouraging $12,500 daily for a trip to the east Mediterranean by a charterer who had an early position to cover.

title: Capesize
summary: A bleak outlook for the big ships with the list of spot ships growing daily and even when most hoped that rates could not go lower, they did. The key West Australia/China rate was now hovering in the low $4.00 range (down from $5.00 pre-holidays) with little prospect of recovery.

title: Panamax
summary: A steady flow of Atlantic enquiry earlier this week did little to prevent falls in rates with current spot ships adding to the list of spot ships overhanging from before the holidays. Charterers were able to fix voyage business and aps rates with little effort.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: The first full week back from the holiday period meant difficult trading conditions for owners in most areas. Tonnage supply outweighed demand in the South Atlantic where it was reported that a 2005 built 56,000 dwt unit spot off south Brazil had been booked for a trip to Singapore-Japan at $11,100 daily plus a ballast bonus of $125,000.

title: Capesize
summary: A week of slight peaks and troughs with the market struggling to maintain gains. In the East the majors were again in the market for West Australia/China cargoes and rates climbed off the lows.

title: Panamax
summary: The Atlantic market continued to weaken with transatlantic mineral cargoes in short supply and insufficient fronthaul business from the US Gulf to the East to lend any support to the market. Cargoes dried up for first half February cargoes with aggressive numbers talked going forward.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Another very difficult week for owners in all areas with evidence appearing that with the lack of business, some are scrambling to fix whatever they can just to keep their tonnage moving. In the US Gulf a 2008 built 58,700 dwt vessel was reported to have been booked for a trip to India with petcoke at around $13,000 daily.

title: Capesize
summary: The market was dormant for the first half of the week and while it had woken up somewhat by the end, levels are still dire. Minimal changes across all the routes with the two main ore voyages from Brazil and west Australia closing at a few cents under where the levels were last week.

title: Panamax
summary: Lunar New Year celebrations where in full swing this week, which led to a quiet market. However this did not seem to have dampened the little green shoots growing slowly throughout the week and it will be interesting going forward with the return to work stations next week if this will continue or wither.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: The Chinese New Year holidays resulted in a minimal amount of business being concluded within the Pacific basin. There was a knock on effect to the Atlantic with brokers struggling to find firm business to fix.

title: Capesize
summary: The Chinese return to work failed to produce any fireworks but a flurry of fixing from the Australian miners, together with slightly firmer bunker prices and some recent weather delays, prompted a further rise in rates in the more active west Australia/China market. The week closed out with talk of BHP Billiton fixing a 29 February 170,000 tonne 10% cargo from Port Hedland to Qingdao at $3.15.

title: Panamax
summary: South American grain shipments continued to underpin the market with rates here firmer over the week. However, going forward views varied and changed frequently.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: The BDI goes back over ‘300' this week, with rates in general all trying to improve over last done and brokers having a busy time with more cargoes in the market. The supramax index nudged up every day this week.

title: Capesize
summary: Very little change for the big ships with rates still at historically low levels. Over the week rates slipped on some routes but as the week closed out there were slight improvement on some routes.

title: Panamax
summary: South America remained the focus for the market determining rates both in the Atlantic and the East. Added to this, significant delays in Brazil were keeping ships off the market longer.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: Under the circumstances, it was a good week for supramax and ultramax markets rates up on the last done and index routes up on a daily basis. Brokers remained uncertain how long this would last but sentiment was positive and driving the market.

title: Capesize
summary: Rates flip-flopped around five cents up or five cents down and this about sums up the capesize market this week. The key West Australia/China run nudged up to $3.00 earlier this week and slipped back to $2.90-95 for 20-24 March positions.

title: Panamax
summary: South American grain cargoes once again dominated activity and helped underpin rates in many areas of the market. The emphasis this week was largely on ships loading April cargoes with much of the front-haul business for March now covered.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: At the risk of sounding repetitive, it has been another good week for supramax owners with a daily increase on the BDI and nearly all individual routes witnessing a positive change. Rates in both theatres tended to show an increase on those last achieved with some talk about period fixtures, although very sketchy for now with details unavailable for reporting.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, rates peaked, with WS 72.5 said to have been fixed by SPC for a short run to Singapore. It was also reported that WS 70 fixed to Malacca.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates have largely held steady throughout the week at WS 92.5 for UK-Cont discharge while in the Black Sea rates have edged down modestly from WS 110 to close to WS 105. In the Mediterranean, Bahri split a VLCC cargo and took two Gungen ships for 135,000 tonnes to Rotterdam at WS 87.5 and 90 while good levels of enquiry and fixing for long haul trips from Caribbean, Med and Black Sea going east have helped thin the tonnage lists.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, a clear out of the early tonnage and sustained enquiry has seen rates rise with WS 112.5 having been agreed for Black Sea loading and Minerva tonnage obtained WS 107.5 for Libya loading. There remains further upward pressure here as bad weather and uncertainty on itineraries for tonnage in Trieste take their toll.

title: Panamaxes
summary: It has been a good week for Panamax owners. In the Caribbean the market has continued to firm with levels here rising to WS 145 for 50,000 tonnes and this has led to ballasters for Uk-Cont fixing locally instead.

title: Clean
summary: Despite some increased activity on the TC2 routes, rates have remained fairly similar over the week at around WS 147 level for 37,000 tonnes. Although the 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK-Cont has been less active this week, rates here appear stable at WS 95 thanks to steady enquiry and fixing to Brazil and West coast Central America, which has been absorbing much of the tonnage.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, the New Year started with good activity leading to rates for 270,000 tonnes going east increasing from WS 60 to a shade above WS 70. With bunker prices continuing to fall, this is a timecharter equivalent of about $70,000 per day.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates dropped significantly at the start of the week, falling from around WS 105 and have now bottomed out at WS 92.5 which has been repeated several times, but there is now again a firmer sentiment in the market, aided also by an active Caribbean/transatlantic market. In the Black Sea rates quickly dropped from low WS 120s to WS 100 but here also rates have started to climb again, with the last seen here being Centrofin tonnage covering a Transway cargo at WS 110 basis 140,000 tonnes.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, it has been a tough week for owners - rates dipped from previous levels of WS 92.5 to WS 87.5 but after healthy levels of enquiry helped clear out a lot of the early tonnage, levels have crept back to stand at between WS 90/92.5. In the Baltic, rates have firmed from low WS 130s at the start of the week for 100,000 tonnes to WS 145, as the ice season gets started, while the 80,000 tonne cross North Sea market has remained steady all week around the WS 120 level.

title: Panamaxes
summary: Status quo here as levels for 55,000 tonnes to the US Gulf have been holding steady at WS 132.5/135.

title: Clean
summary: Despite an active week, MRs on the Continent going transatlantic for 37,000 tonnes have eased, with recent rates being fixed region WS 147 which is down from WS 175 a week ago. While the market for 38,000 tonne cargoes USG to Continent continues to soften, standing at around WS 90 and remains under downward pressure.

title: VLCCs
summary: Rates in the Middle East Gulf have held around WS 67.50-70 level for 270,000 tonnes to South Korea/China. For trades going west Bahri managed to cover 280,000 tonnes to the US Gulf on two ships early this week at WS 35/36 (cape/cape basis), but later in the week Litasco reportedly took Athenian tonnage from Basrah for west options only at WS 42 (cape/cape), although they would have paid some premium for the options.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: Rates for West Africa to Continent after initially holding at WS 92.5 came under pressure as tonnage numbers increased. Consequently Total were able to conclude at a lower WS 88.75 although it is now believed this deal may have failed on subjects.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, an active start to the week saw rates firm considerably with the week's high being WS 165, although this was for Libya load which incurs a premium due to the current political problems. Thereafter levels peaked at around WS 140 and rates are now coming under pressure as suezmaxes struggle and seek coverage also by playing the aframax market accordingly.

title: Panamaxes
summary: It has been a good week for panamax owners with levels being fixed around WS 155 for 55,000 tonne cargoes from Continent to the US Gulf and ice business from Baltic/transatlantic paying WS 170 plus.

title: Clean
summary: It has been a disappointing week for owners as a lack of enquiry combined with a build-up of tonnage has seen levels for MR tonnage fall from WS 142.5 at the start of the week to barely WS 130 and lower levels likely. The 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK-Cont has also struggled with rates easing from WS 92.5 down to low WS 80s.

title: VLCCs
summary: With open tonnage building up and fewer cargoes available, Middle East Gulf rates have been under pressure. In the last month it seems over 30 vessels have fixed on timecharter basis for various short to long term periods, with some now being marketed on the spot market.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa rates fell away quickly with WS 75 and WS77.5 being paid for US Gulf and USAC respectively. However rates are on their way back up again with Petrogal taking tonnage at both WS 80 and also WS 82.5.

title: Aframaxes
summary: There was an active start to the week in the Mediterranean which enabled owners to halt the slide with WS 115 being agreed. Thereafter some tricky cargoes with tight dates saw WS 120 paid and a short voyage from Algeria eventually went at WS 145.

title: Panamaxes
summary: Although levels here eased slightly with WS 147.5 now on subjects for Cont/US Gulf, basis 55,000 tonnes, a strong Caribs/up coast panamax market is enticing tonnage to stay local rather than ballast and brokers feel charterers will now have their work cut out to repeat this number.

title: Clean
summary: It has been a tough week for owners as the market dropped sharply from WS 130 down to barely WS 115 but a thinning of tonnage and improved levels of enquiry have helped stem the fall and with some outstanding enquiry, there is again a slightly firmer sentiment in the market. The 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK-Cont is on its knees with levels having crashed from WS 80 a week ago down to WS 55.

title: VLCCs
summary: At the start of the week, rates in the Middle East Gulf went in to freefall as a combination of surplus tonnage and a light February programme took their toll. With the oil price up around $10 a barrel, storage interest would appear to have waned and a number of ships taken on timecharter appeared as relets.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, owners have enjoyed a good week with rates continuing their upward trend from the end of last week. WS 100 has been done on more than one occasion, although there is now a rumour of WS 93 having just been agreed.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, owners have been firmly in the driving seat with rates jumping sharply up now to WS 200. A combination of bad weather and an increase in Turkish straits delays have combined to put charterers under pressure as they seek tonnage with a reliable itinerary.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to US Gulf has held steady here at WS 147.5 basis 55,000 tonnes.

title: Clean
summary: Owners have had to face another tough week here with levels for 37,000 tonnes from Continent/USAC stagnant at WS 115, and West Africa discharge paying WS 135. The 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK-Cont has slumped to WS 50.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf rates have been in gentle decline as I.P. week has kicked in, with less of the recent volatility.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: Rates from West Africa continue to soften. After Total and Petrogal both covered at WS 85, Cepsa are understood to have agreed WS 81.5 for a short trip to Spain, and there is now a report of WS 77.5 having been agreed for UK-Cont discharge by Petroineos on the Petalidi while Exxon are understood to have taken ‘DHT Trader' on subs at WS 72.5 for US Gulf discharge.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, rates have crashed as charterers were inundated with offers including suezmaxes on part cargoes. Whereas a week ago, the market was in the WS 190s, owners are now willing levels around WS 122.5 and Black Sea is understood to have been covered at WS 115.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to the US Gulf has been under pressure with re-let tonnage available and sparse enquiry levels have dropped around 7.5 WS points to WS 140 basis 55,000 tonnes as owners just look to keep their tonnage moving.

title: Clean
summary: Rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent/USAC fluctuated with a drop of around 10 points early in the week to around WS 100, although rates have now edged back up very modestly to around WS 105. The 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK-Cont spluttered back in to life and rates rose steadily to almost WS 70 before a build-up of tonnage for 15/20 February window saw levels slip back to around WS 62.5, although this is still a good 10 points better than this time last week.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, rates have remained under pressure as the February program is completed. March fixing so far has been slow and the owners' cause is not being helped by Chinese New Year celebrations.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: Although P66 had to pay WS 82.5 to the US Gulf for a replacement cargo loading 22 February, rates from West Africa have in general moved sideways with US Gulf discharge being covered at WS 72.5. There is also a report of Tesoro taking the Pecos for a trip to Chiriquigrande at WS 70.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, it has been another disappointing week for owners. Normally with bad weather, Turkish straits delays and Trieste berth maintenance, these would be the ideal ingredients for the market to push up but a dearth of enquiry has seen tonnage build up and charterers have been able to sit back and watch levels drop further to WS 90/95 with Black Sea aframax rates also at WS 95 level.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to the US Gulf has remained under pressure as coa business and own program has left little for market tonnage to look at. Although there is only limited tonnage for February, the dearth of enquiry sees levels being evaluated at around WS 130 for 55,000 tonnes.

title: Clean
summary: The arb for gasoil and gasoline opened up this week. Very cold weather on US East Coast and a flood of enquiry which quickly thinned out the tonnage list saw rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent/USAC surge from WS 105 a week ago to WS 140.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, it has been another slow week and rates continued to ease. Brokers are suggesting the lighter amount of business is partially because of tonnage previously taken on period/storage now loading and eating in to the normal volumes, which is creating nervousness amongst owners.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, it has been a better week for owners. An active Caribs/up coast market absorbed significant levels of tonnage, thus thinning the West Africa list as charterers looked to cover their second decade cargoes.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, a very busy start to the week saw around 25 ships go on subjects. Despite this activity, rates hardly moved as the massive surplus of tonnage put paid to any over enthusiasm from owners.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to the US Gulf has remained under pressure. There was a report of WS 125 being agreed, but this was for a ship back-loading in the same port, so no ballast involved.

title: Clean
summary: The market has continued to firm as the prolonged cold spell in USAC leads to sustained demand. With increased enquiry for Nigeria discharge as well, this has led to a tight tonnage list and rates have continued to climb all week, with WS 170 now being on subjects basis 37,000 tonnes cargo quantity.

title: VLCCs
summary: Not surprisingly the market remained largely unchanged due to the combination of International Petroleum week and Chinese New Year. February program is now covered with long east rates for 270,000 tonnes maintained in the low WS 60s and west rates hovering between WS 34.50/36 level.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: A slow start to the week saw rates in the low WS 70s for Europe discharge but a replacement cargo led to pressure on the market. Further increased levels of enquiry significantly tightened the tonnage list and rates increased sharply with reports of WS 95 having now been paid for an Angola/Portugal run.

title: Aframaxes
summary: It has been a much better week for owners in the Mediterranean, as plenty of enquiry finally thinned what had previously been a bloated tonnage list. Activity in Black Sea was also strong and rates moved around 7.5 WS points to high WS 80s in the Mediterranean with low/mid WS 90s now paid from Black Sea.

title: Panamaxes
summary: Off the Continent, it has been an uneventful week with the market steady in the low/mid WS 120s for 55,000 tonnes from ARA back to the US Gulf.

title: Clean
summary: A quiet week on the continent/USAC market saw rates initially ease 2.5 WS points to WS 112.5 for 37,000 tonnes, and there was even a report of WS 107.5 having been agreed but levels now are looking more settled at around WS 112.5. In the US Gulf backhaul trade, healthy amounts of enquiry, albeit predominantly for short-haul trade to the Caribbean/central and South America led to a thinner tonnage list, which has created a significant firming of rates.

title: VLCCs
summary: It has been an uneventful week in the Middle East Gulf with the market holding steady in the low WS 60s basis 270,000 tonnes for long east, and west rates recovered to around WS 34.50/35 having fallen to WS 31.5 earlier. A relatively modest surplus of February tonnage, aided by ullage and weather delays in China, has kept the levels steady, with West Africa absorbing some of the tonnage here.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: After last week's upswing in West Africa, rates have come under pressure as a consequence of the VLCC activity. Rates at the start of the week were region WS 97/98, but plentiful tonnage saw rates ease first to WS 90, and then Petrogal covered a run to Portugal at WS 85.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, rates have held steady in the mid/high WS 90s. With a number of ships presently on subjects and good levels of enquiry from both east and west Mediterranean, combined with an active Black Sea market, brokers feel there is potential for the market to firm further.

title: Panamaxes
summary: Off the Continent, it has been a slow week with the Caribs upcoast panamax market falling further to WS 120 level, which is leading to more ballasters coming across. There is no shortage of tonnage looking to fix from ARA back to the US Gulf, with rates here under pressure at around WS 120 for 55,000 tonnes and the potential to ease further.

title: Clean
summary: A busy start to the week flattered to deceive and rates have remained steady on the Continent/USAC trade in the WS 110/115 region. There was a deal done by Statoil at WS 120, but this was for Mongstad loading which tends to pay a premium over ARA.

title: VLCCs
summary: It has been another difficult week in the Middle East Gulf as a plentiful supply of tonnage has enabled charterers to maintain pressure on owners. A couple of runs to Taiwan and Thailand were covered just below WS 50, albeit on 15/16 year old tonnage.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, the market has been flat. Rates eased initially a couple of points to settle at WS 67.5 for Europe while WS 62.5 was agreed for US Gulf discharge.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, a Sidi Kerir to Portugal enquiry set the tone as Petrogal covered here at WS 70, representing a new low for this year. Others were enticed in to the market on the back of this but were unable to repeat this level and the market has now settled around WS 80 for Cross Med with Black Sea tending to pay around WS 85.

title: Panamaxes
summary: Off the Continent, with the VGO arb closed, it has been another difficult week with limited enquiry and rates from ARA to the US Gulf under pressure. Brokers feel some owners may now be willing to consider breaking WS 100 here.

title: Clean
summary: In the 37,000 tonnes Cont/USAC trade, there is a sense of déjà vu with rates largely unchanged, still hovering between WS 112.5/115. In the US Gulf backhaul trade, the market has held steady throughout the week at around WS 120 which may yet benefit the Continent/Transatlantic trade as owners prefer to ballast down rather than head back to ARA.

title: CHAPTER 2 - Tramp Shipping
summary:
DURING the half century which ended in 1914, most
of the transoceanic cargoes of coal, ores, and grain were carried in
comparatively small, general-purpose cargo ships. Moving as they
did on routings which varied from voyage to voyage, hauling now
one commodity and then another, entering and leaving port with
out fanfare or publicity, and often in need of paint, these vessels
gained the appellation of "tramp steamers." To the extent that their
wanderings and unkempt appearance paralleled those of that fra
ternity of homeless men known as "tramps," the sobriquet may
have been appropriate.

INTRODUCTION
THE SCOPE OF THE BOOK
Following the seminal work of Tinbergen (1931, 1934) and Koopmans (1939)
research in maritime economics has focused on integrating the various markets
into a dynamic system. This macroeconomic or systems approach to maritime
economics reached its heyday with the Beenstock-Vergottis (BV) model (1993).

tages. The first relates to the microfoundations of the freight market and the
second to the microfoundations of the shipyard and secondhand markets.

From a statistical point of view fluctuations in economic activity, called business
cycles, are generated by random shocks, such as abrupt and sustained oil price
changes or productivity improvements. These shocks can be either transitory or
permanent.

THE FINANCIALISATION
OF SHIPPING MARKETS
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
In the 1950s and 1960s, business cycles in the US and other industrialised
countries were demand-led. The stabilisation of the economy around potential
output was, on the whole, successful through demand management (fiscal and/
or monetary policy).

title: THE FINANCIALISATION OF SHIPPING MARKETS 273

in 2003, with its gradual rise to pre-eminence in world trade, signalled the advent

tanker and the dry markets. The structural change means that the interaction of
demand and supply is insufficient to explain fluctuations in freight rates.

title: THE FINANCIALISATION OF SHIPPING MARKETS 275
summary:

supply-led, they have been asset-led driven by liquidity. Asset-led business cycles,
like the last two cycles in the US, or those experienced by Japan in the 1990s or
the US in the 1930s, produce a larger variability in output than in inflation.

INVESTMENT STRATEGY
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The investment strategy implications of this book are that an owner should have
the optimum fleet and be in the spot market during a bull shipping market; and
should keep the fleet at a minimum to cover fixed expenses and be in the period
market during a bear shipping market. The strategy switches at the turning points
of the shipping cycle.

The development of maritime history as a specialized field of research is

Economic History Association.1 Skip Fischer's own publications, together
with his relentless efforts as editor of theInternational Journal of Maritime
History, have contributed significantly to placing seaborne transport
at the centre of the international economic history of the nineteenth
century. As a result of the collective efforts made in the field since the
1970s, most economists, economic historians and general historians

ing a truly global economy before World War One (WWI).

Introduction
From the vantage point of the twenty-first century the history of
Britain's shipping over the previous century may seem one of a long
process of decline - ‘ebb tide' in the words of one historian.1 In 1900
approaching half of the world's tonnage was under the British flag. In 2000 British owners' share of world shipping, whether vessels were
registered in the UK or elsewhere, was 2.58%, putting it in tenth place.2
This change in Britain's maritime status was not, however, a gradual
process.

Introduction
The Australian and New Zealand port industries in the post-World
War II period exhibit strong elements of path dependence. Simply
put, economic and political actors' purposive decisions pushed the
development of port institutions down a pathway which became hard
to step off: institutional lock-ins impeded strategic flexibility and
the growth of port productivity; inefficient macro- and micro-level
institutional arrangements reduced Australian and New Zealand port
efficiency.

summary: The analysis suggests that in a market with a tight supply/demand balance rate moves can be quite volatile. It appears that just as a combination of greater ship availability and falling fixture activity led to a fall in rates at the end of December, less tanker availability and rising fixture activity has resulted in, well, let's see, a rise in rates.

Rates seem to have paused their ascent though but will probably stay strong in the near term as long as the tonnage supply picture remains tight and crude oil liftings from the Arabian Gulf and West Africa keep on growing.

title: Crude Inventories - Friend or Foe to Tankers?
section_path: Crude Inventories - Friend or Foe to Tankers?
section_path_text: Crude Inventories - Friend or Foe to Tankers?
summary: The most recent OPEC Monthly Oil Market Report (www.opec.org) listing of world oil inventories shows an uptrend, but does this presage a potential cutback in tanker cargoes if there is a return to "normalcy," given relatively flat oil consumption in Western Europe and OECD Pacific regions and marked increases in North American consumption? There are two general types of inventory- inventory held by commercial interests and government sponsored Strategic Petroleum Reserves.

title: North America
summary: Western Europe OECD Pacific A closer scrutiny of the data shows that North America commercial inventory has remained fairly flat with little change between 1997 and 2004. Oil inventories in Western Europe increased by just under 30 million barrels since 1997, which was compensated by a nearly equal decline in inventories in OECD Pacific (Japan, Korea, Australia, and New Zealand).

title: OECD Pacific Days
summary: Western Europe Days North America Days OECD Pacific Inv Western Europe Inv North America Inv While oil companies have been keeping inventories fairly level, SPRs have been growing. The SPR in North America (United States) has increased by 110 million barrels since 1997; Western Europe has increased by 35 million barrels, as has OECD Pacific (Japan).

title: OECD Pacific Days
summary: Western Europe Days North America Days OECD Pacific Inv Western Europe Inv North America Inv Inventories cover uncertainties. For oil companies, the chief uncertainty is associated with demand whereas governments' focus on uncertainty is associated with supply.

title: Days of Inventory
summary: Inv On Land Inv On the Water Total land inventories have climbed 160 million barrels since 1997 plus another 80 million barrels increase in floating inventory, which of course reflects a greater volume of global oil flows. The overall impact has been a reduction in total inventories from 83 days of consumption to 80 days of consumption since 1997.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: Surface Calm - Hidden Undercurrents The volume of Suezmax spot fixtures has been around 2,100 since 2000 other than for a dip in 2001. But there have been changes in where Suezmaxes have been loading.

These have been more or less balanced by a decline in the number of UKC and Caribbean fixtures.

title: B.Sea/Med
summary: Black Sea/Mediterranean Load Area in First Place The increased number of liftings out of the Black Sea and North Africa is now greater than the number of liftings out of West Africa. West Africa, which held first place since 2000, is now in second place.

This decline in ton-mile demand is partly compensated by a rising long haul trade to the United States from 3 fixtures in 2000 to 50 in 2004.

title: Other
summary: Carib ECSA UKC Med USA The United States has been picking up the slack from the fall-off in fixtures to the UKC and Mediterranean as Caspian crude backs out West African crude in Europe. Fixture activity to East Coast South America, primarily Brazil, has declined as Brazilian domestic (offshore) production moves the nation closer to self-sufficiency.

summary: W of Suez Australia SE Asia S Asia China&FE As China's economy continues to expand, Suezmaxes will see increasing business to move crude to ports that cannot accommodate VLCCs. summary: Americans don't seem to know a thing about Economics 101- they violate all the rules! They buy more as prices climb and buy less when prices fall.

title: The Bullwhip Effect
summary: The bullwhip effect is a phenomenon noticed in supply chains where the failure of a buyer to communicate nothing but a spastic order now and then creates an increasing degree of disorder as orders cascade from the first tier supplier to second and third-tier suppliers, and beyond, increasing inventory throughout the chain. If the buyer communicates the actual production schedule to the suppliers, then the suppliers have the information necessary to adjust their production to actual demand, significantly reducing inventory.

title: Getting Back to (Inventory) Basics?
summary: In the good ol' days, the purpose of oil inventories was to cover contingencies and uncertainties. Greater amounts of inventory on hand meant greater coverage to mitigate the risk of supply interruptions.

title: Days in Inventory
summary: The average inventory of crude oil since 1990 has been 318 million barrels and the average days of consumption in inventory 22.2 days. Both the volume of inventory and the days of inventory on hand have been in a general decline, reflecting a changing attitude towards inventory from that of an asset to a cost.

title: Days in Inventory
summary: Gasoline inventories have a much greater seasonal swing than crude oil as they are generally accumulated in the spring in anticipation of the peak summer driving season. Thus gasoline inventories in the United States are a buffer against seasonal demand.

title: Days in Inventory
summary: Also similar to gasoline, overall inventory has remained about the same, averaging 121.7 million barrels since 1990. However, there has also been a significant decline in days of consumption in inventory from about 41 days in the early 1990s to 27 days in recent years for an overall average of 35.8 days.

title: Jet Fuel
summary: Jet fuel (kerosene) has shown the least change both in the volume of inventory and in the degree of decline in days of consumption in inventory. Average inventories have been 41 million barrels whereas days of consumption has declined from about 32 days in the early 1990s to a current level of about 25 days since the mid 1990s.

title: So What's the Story?
summary: There appears to be some reversion back to inventory as a means to mitigate the risk of supply interruptions and away from acting as a sink for corporate capital. Indeed a contango market permits oil companies to hedge against accumulating high priced crude oil if indeed the present run up in crude prices should falter.

title: Peak Oil? Not in Kuwait!
summary: The issue of peak oil has received considerable attention over the past year or so as crude prices remain significantly above their long term averages. One country that is taking action to be sure that the world is not running out of oil is Kuwait.

title: In The Beginning
summary: Kuwait's geographic location at the top of the Arabian Gulf helped establish the country as a trading hub. Oil was first discovered in the 1930s and the first export of crude oil was in 1946.

title: Keeping up the Pace
summary: With estimated reserves at about 100 billion barrels, Kuwait holds about 10% of the world's reserves. Despite producing over 2.0 million barrels per day for the past several years, the proven reserves have remained steady.

title: Ambitious Plans - Project Kuwait
summary: Kuwait's primary fields are those known as Greater Burgan and those fields under exploration in the North of the country. Greater Burgan is thought to be the second largest deposit of oil in the world.

title: Key Role in Refining

summary: The cost of bunker fuel has always been a central component of determining a tanker's earnings, and in recent weeks, rising fuel costs have once again come to complicate an already‐challenging tanker market. Faced with surging fuel prices at a time of weak earnings and depressed demand, owners currently mired in the summer doldrums find themselves asking: what's causing the rise in bunker prices and how long can it be sustained?

The narrowing differential between light and heavy crude oils is playing a leading role in the recent rise in the cost of bunker fuel. As sources of heavy crude oil production hold back for whatever reason, refineries configured to process these traditionally less‐ expensive heavy oils have been forced to pay higher prices.

title: AG ‐ FE (260kt)
summary: % Fuel Cost While the factors contributing to the recent rise in bunker prices are relatively easy to identify, determining how long they will continue to push prices up is difficult. Owners currently watching fuel costs sap already diminished earnings may be well served to learn about the factors currently pushing up bunker prices.

title: Going With the Flow
summary: Last week, 500,000 bbls of Colombian Castilla blend crude oil flowed through the Petroterminal de Panama (PTP) pipeline in Panama. The cargo was the pipeline's first to flow from east to west and the reversal in flow direction mirrors a shift in petroleum trading patterns from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

title: Argentina
summary: The pipeline is primarily expected to help provide refiners on the US West Coast with a wider variety of crude oils. Tesoro signed a seven‐year agreement last December to ship 107 kbd through the reversed pipeline in order to supply its five largest refineries, located in California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.

title: Reading Tea Leaves
summary: After last year's sudden and dramatic wrecking of the world's economies, the sterling perception of economic theory has become severely tarnished. Despite this fall from grace, some economists have lately been talking of the signs of a nascent recovery.

Governments worldwide are working both separately and together to develop limits on sulfur and carbon emissions from industry, improvements in mileage standards for automobiles and better oversight of derivatives trading.

title: Single and Waiting to Mingle
summary: Heading into the fourth quarter, it is becoming apparent that 2009 is not shaping up to be the pivotal year as many had expected regarding the single hull fleet. Some shipowners hoped that the planned removal of single hull tankers would have provided support to freight rates and asset prices this year.

title: On Incident
summary: Prior to the Hebei Spirit incident in December 2007, South Korea was generally expected to allow non‐double hull tankers to trade in its ports through 2015. South Korea had long been the top discharge port for the single hull tankers that were the subject of International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations requiring the vessels stop trading by 2015.

title: Making the Market
summary: The economics supporting the continued trade in single hull tankers are being seriously tested in the current market. Historically, the advantage offered by single hull tankers was that they traded at a discount compared to their double hulled counterparts.

title: Differential
summary: AG‐FE (260kt) DH AG‐FE (260kt) Non‐DH Lower capital expenses of single hull tankers has enabled shipowners to keep the older ships operational until the practice is banned altogether. Shipowners will take their chances and hold onto these ships in hopes they will be the beneficiaries of future market spikes.

title: The Road to Recovery
summary: At the onset of the financial crisis last year, the fourth quarter of 2009 was targeted as the likely beginning of a recovery in the international economy. With the fourth quarter now upon us, things are, in fact, undeniably less bad than they have been.

summary: 84.4 84.7 0.3 A major factor in China's recent demand growth has been a new pricing regime instituted at the beginning of this year for petroleum products sold domestically. The system guarantees a profit for Chinese refiners and is designed to encourage them to maximize runs, presumably contributing to recent high levels of demand.

title: OECD‐ Back in the Saddle
summary: Recent economic news may suggest things are improving in developed economies but it will take a while for the OECD to fully recover from the 2009's sharp drop‐off in demand. Nevertheless, the IEA sees a short‐term demand increase within both North America and Europe.

title: LCC Monthly Average TCE, $/day
summary: The IEA's recent demand projections suggest a possible restructuring of trade flows that could create modestly more ton‐mile demand during the fourth quarter. While supply and demand fundamentals dictate that the long‐term focus of demand growth will return to the non‐OECD countries, the short‐term improvements in OECD demand present a reason for some hope amid the discouragement that has prevailed for months.

title: A Farewell Contango?
summary: The storage of crude oil and petroleum products at sea has been an important factor in the tanker market throughout 2009. It can be argued that the use of tankers as floating storage by refiners, oil majors, and traders has helped support freight rates by providing term employment for ships in a challenging rate environment.

title: December 2008 Curve
summary: June 2009 Curve September 2009 Curve October 2009 Curve Tanker storage fixtures are typically short‐term time charters ranging from 30 to 90 days, often with the option to be extended longer. Additionally, vessels continue to be fixed on the spot market with storage options attached.

title: Unwinding Contango
summary: A number of factors conspired to make storage beneficial for both charterers and owners this year. In December of 2008, with oil prices low in the aftermath of economic collapse, storage fixtures started to have a noticeable impact on the market.

title: Back to Backwardation?
summary: If contango is in fact winding down, the reasons behind this change could spell mixed news for the tanker market. A reduction in crude oil in floating storage in the immediate future threatens to reduce import needs of long‐haul crude oil by disgorging volumes of nearby oil to waiting refiners while simultaneously reintroducing ships to the market, undoubtedly depressing rates.

title: Polar Express
summary: Last month, retreating sea ice allowed two multipurpose heavy‐lift project carriers to complete a voyage through the Northeast Passage from South Korea, around the Russian Arctic, and on to Rotterdam. Beluga Shipping, the German company whose vessels completed the trip, called it the first non‐Russian commercial voyage through the route.

title: USA
summary: The ships then proceeded along Russia's arctic coast, through the Bering Strait and on to the Siberian port of Novyi, where their cargo was unloaded on September 7. The vessels then left the passage and continued on to Murmansk and further to Rotterdam, which they reached in late September.

title: Murmansk
summary: The vessels' path is shown in the map to the right.

title: Rotterdam
summary: The traditional route takes ships through the South China Sea, past Singapore, around India and through the Suez Canal. Earlier this summer, Norway's foreign minister told an audience in England that the "pirate‐free" route would cut tanker transit times between Europe and Asia by 40 percent within a decade, fueling speculation that the Northeast Passage could emerge as a summertime competitor to the Suez Canal.

title: Eurasia
summary: There may be a time when a constellation of circumstances align to make the Northeast Passage an efficient route for a tanker with a very specific cargo and positioning, but it is unlikely that many owners will react to the recent news by jumping to on the ice class bandwagon. The tanker industry would nonetheless be well‐served to follow developments surrounding the Northeast Passage closely.

title: Barrels Bound East
summary: The rapid growth of China's oil demand has forced a transition from self‐sufficiency enjoyed in the early 1990s toward dependence on imports for about half of its crude oil requirement. Managing their growing import dependence has become a central concern of policy planners in Beijing and an important factor in the development of present and future tanker trade routes.

title: Domestic Production
summary: Consumption In the first half of 2009, as total crude oil consumption fell 3.2 mbd compared with 2008 levels, resilience in the Chinese economy helped stave off a complete collapse in the global economy. A $586 billion stimulus package China launched last year to counteract the impact of the economic crisis was focused on boosting domestic consumption of goods and services.

title: Have Trade, Will Travel
summary: Though some future Chinese imports will be received through pipelines, tanker owners have reason to welcome China's recent energy investments as they will ultimately result in incremental increases in ton‐mile demand. Chinese sponsored exports have already helped transform the West Africa to Far East voyage from a sleepy backhaul into a primary money‐ making voyage and Venezuela's increased exports to China have supported Caribbean to Far East rates.

title: AG ‐ China
summary: AG ‐ US Gulf WAF ‐ China WAF ‐ USAC/US Gulf About half of Chinese crude oil imports come from the Middle East and cargoes bound for China are expected to continue as a major factor in supporting rates out of the Arabian Gulf. Another producer expected to see increased volumes headed for China is Brazil.

title: Wild Card
summary: Perhaps the largest wildcard with respect to the shipping markets will be China's interest in developing a domestic fleet for the transportation of imported barrels. If China takes the reins on shipping, the market for crude oil tankers could become fragmented.

title: Trick or Treat ?
summary: As the Halloween holiday comes creeping in, many shipowners find themselves wondering if the next few weeks will bring a trick or a treat from the markets. The economy in the United States seemed to have received a treat earlier this week when the Department of Commerce reported 3.5 percent economic growth during the third quarter of this year.

title: Better than Candy Corn
summary: While Arabian Gulf liftings headed to the West have remained low, shipowners have been encouraged to keep a weather eye on the fuel oil market originating in the Caribbean and US Gulf. Vessels in the Caribbean can capitalize on the steady trade ferrying fuel oil to China and have become one factor whittling down the number of VLCCs waiting in the Arabian Gulf.

title: CAR/USG ‐ Far East
summary: Stronger earnings on voyages out of West Africa have likely also attracted a few vessels to reposition to that market. Increased slow‐steaming, reportedly of roughly 1‐2 knots, and resulting voyage extensions could also be decreasing the number of vessels competing for cargoes in the Arabian Gulf.

title: Conclusion
summary: While supply fundamentals point to the next phase in a road to recovery‐ slow but steady increases in earnings, the salvation will ultimately lie within the hands of consumers. Demand west of the Arabian Gulf has shown some promise over the past quarter as GDP growth has proved economists wrong.

title: Leveraging Flat Rates
summary: Each year, the Worldscale Association adjusts the flat rates which serve as the starting point for negotiating the cost of carrying crude oil and refined products on tankers. Under normal conditions, this annual revision ritual does not have a dramatic impact on tanker markets, aside from forcing owners and charterers to adjust to the new rates during the first weeks of the year.

title: AG ‐ LOOP
summary: The rising price of bunkers has been the central force driving the annual bumps in Worldscale flat rates in recent years. The Worldscale bunker assumption is an average of assessments of 380 cSt bunker fuel between October 1 to September 30 provided by LQM Petroleum Services.

title: HFO
summary: In addition to adjustments for bunker prices, the annual rate revisions to Worldscale rates are also designed to reflect changes in port costs and transit fees. This year, Worldscale opted to retain its language relating to existing Emissions Control Areas and announced it will make allowances at all EU ports for cost of 0.1% sulfur, which will be required from January 1, 2010 in compliance with the EU Sulphur Directive.

title: A Medium Term Outlook
summary: Tanker Prospects 2010 - 2014 A Medium Term Outlook Any attempt to project the course of the tanker market between now and 2014 must confront its position at the crossroads of so many of the challenges currently facing the worldwide economy. Changing trade and consumption patterns, ever‐tightening environmental regulation and the pace of global economic recovery must all be considered alongside the other fundamentals long assumed to propel crude oil and tanker markets.

title: VLCC Spot Market Earnings
summary: Foremost among the uncertainties currently facing the tanker market is the pace of orderbook deliveries. As in past downturns, the delivery of vessels ordered at the height of the market continues to hold down freight rates still struggling to recover.

title: Already in Ship Shape
summary: Late last month, a malfunctioning valve on the barge supplying a product tanker reportedly caused it to spill between 400 and 800 gallons (between 9 and 19 barrels) of bunker fuel into San Francisco Bay. The spill reignited an environmental group's campaign for a ban on the use of residual bunker fuel, an effort initiated following the Cosco Busan spill in 2007.

title: >700 Tonnes
summary: The ITOPF has tracked accidental spills by tankers, combined carriers and barges since 1974. The group categorizes small spills as those involving less than 7 tons, medium‐sized spills as between 7 and 700 tons and large spills (as mentioned) as anything exceeding 700 tons.

title: Metric Tons Spilled
summary: Well‐intentioned as it may be, there are several problems with responding to the recent spill with a ban on the use of residual bunker fuel. Primarily, this initiative ignores the ongoing tightening of marine fuel regulation which is already underway.

title: Talking Turkey
summary: For many in the tanker industry, 2009 has been a tough year. Shipowners and charterers alike can commiserate about low demand for crude oil and refined products as well as the limping pace of growth in many economies.

title: ......And Seasons Go
summary: Aside from fluctuations in demand, volatility in the tanker market can be divided into two broad categories; unforeseen delays and psychology of market participants. While the extreme volatility that drove the market to new highs in late 2007 and early 2008 has receded, participants in the tanker industry should continue expecting the unexpected.

title: Happy Thanksgiving!
summary: While it is easy for some shipowners to look back fondly on the perfect storm of surging demand and tight tonnage which began just before Thanksgiving 2007, 2009 rate trends have served as a reminder that what comes up, must come down. An additional reminder to those participating in tomorrow's holiday; resist the temptation to take a post‐dinner nap, you could just miss a jump in the market!

title: Surviving Whammies
summary: US refiners are being forced to deal with dismal margins brought about by a lack of demand for their prime products - gasoline and diesel. Consumption of gasoline is roughly 7 percent less than the go‐go days of mid‐2007 - and once the growth in ethanol use is considered, the need for refiners' hydrocarbon component has contracted even more.

title: Motor Gasoline
summary: Distillate Fuel Oil Over the last few years, the cumulative impact of lower product demand and greater mandated use of biofuels has raised the level of idle US refining capacity. Even when the recently announced closures of the Sunoco New Jersey and Valero Delaware refineries are reflected in operable capacity, the capacity glut remains above the levels of just a few years ago unless more refinery closures occur.

title: Refinery Inputs
summary: Refinery Operable Capacity Idle Capacity The Renewable Fuel Standard dictates that by 2022 the inclusion of biofuels in gasoline must increase nearly three‐fold from 2009's mandated level of 11.1 billion gallons per year (685 kbd). Faced with the prospect of over 1.3 mbd additional biofuel being included in gasoline as well as improving vehicle fleet fuel efficiency, a US refiner may see little reason to expand their ability to produce more hydrocarbon‐based fuel.

title: The Coup de grâce?
summary: US rules on limiting domestic GHG emissions are still wending their way through the legislative process. But judging by the volume of complaints emanating from segments of the refining industry, one might conclude that the rules proposed by the country's august legislators are less than fair and equitable to all parties affected.

title: GHG Legislation Forming, Tanker Owners Take Warning
section_path: GHG Legislation Forming, Tanker Owners Take Warning
section_path_text: GHG Legislation Forming, Tanker Owners Take Warning
summary: The seemingly endless line of storm clouds gathering around US refiners does not appear to bode well for people trying to make a living carrying crude oil to the shores of this nation. While domestic refining capacity in a few niche markets may weather the pending GHG allocation storm, some of those located in markets with easy access to imports may become pressured financially and eventually succumb.

title: Still in the Dark in Denmark
section_path: Still in the Dark in Denmark
section_path_text: Still in the Dark in Denmark
summary: In the weeks and months leading up to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Copenhagen, expectations ran high that the meeting would produce a concrete emissions‐reduction framework to replace that of the Kyoto Protocol. As the discussions progress, it becomes more apparent that a resolution may not be forthcoming.

title: Rest of World: 10,292
summary: President Obama hopes Copenhagen will produce a new framework that includes legally binding emissions‐reduction targets for developing countries, especially China and India. It was the lack of such binding targets for developing countries which prevented Congressional approval of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol.

title: Intensely Level Playing Field
summary: China has tried to change the metric for measuring progress on emissions reduction from total emissions to one of emissions intensity. The concept of carbon intensity measures emissions per unit of GDP and allows China to highlight that while it is the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter by volume, it has much lower per capita emissions than the United States and other industrialized countries.

title: GDP Per Capita
summary: The European Union has announced it will provide $150 billion to developing nations each year through 2020 and proposed a system under which poorer countries would be legally required to take specific actions as developed countries continue to work towards assigned national targets. Earlier this year, China suggested that developed nations commit one percent of their GDP to developing countries' efforts to limit their emissions.

title: Its Only Money
summary: When the Copenhagen conference began, industrialized countries responded by endorsing a proposal for a $10 billion per year fund to be transferred to developing countries to help them with the potential impact of climate change. In the opening days of the conference, the White House said a consensus was forming around the idea, which it said would form a core element of any agreement produced in Copenhagen.

title: Can This Ever Work ?
summary: In a press release for its Annual Energy Outlook, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) candidly acknowledges that the United States is unlikely to meet long‐term biofuels blending targets. Significant doubts also remain as to whether or not the United States will even be able to produce the level of biofuels mandated for blending next year.

title: Corn Ethanol
summary: This past March, an application for a waiver to raise the maximum allowable ethanol content in gasoline from 10 to 15 percent was submitted by a coalition of ethanol producers. The coalition's proposal was an effort to help their struggling industry, which is threatened by dropping gasoline demand and the auto parc's move towards more efficient vehicles.

title: Great Expectations
summary: One of the reasons the EIA expects the US to fall short of the goals set forth in the original RFS is that they were formulated on assumptions of continued technological progress in the development of non‐grain, "second generation" cellulosic biofuels. Cellulosic biofuels are those derived from renewable biomass feedstocks such as fast growing grasses, cereal straw and forest residues among others.

title: No Water Left Behind
summary: During his campaign, President Obama called for higher volumes of advanced biofuels partially to ensure the overall sustainability of the biofuels program. Now it appears that the program is coming under greater scrutiny.

title: Conclusion
summary: The apparent stalemate in Copenhagen serves as a reminder of the need to balance aspirations with practicality when crafting sweeping policies for a less carbon‐intensive economy. Aggressive biofuels targets were set deliberately to push the industry forward, but the emerging challenges facing the ethanol industry highlights the need to reexamine the assumptions which underpin current policy.

title: Stocking Slippage
summary: This time last year, the tanker market found itself partially insulated from the pressures being felt in other shipping sectors, but nevertheless many remained fearful that 2009 would see the market wracked by cancellations and bank failures. While the past year has certainly been challenging for tankers, the worst sale and purchase market fears have yet to materialize.

title: Second Hand
summary: New Building After years of relatively easy access to financing from banks, liquidity problems in the wake of the economic crisis brought sale and purchase activity to a virtual standstill in early 2009. Many owners were forced to negotiate waivers and extensions of existing debt covenants.

title: Orderbook Impact
summary: Worsening sentiment in the sale and purchase market also had an impact on those invested in the looming orderbook. With owners who placed orders at shipyards during boom years experiencing liquidity problems, the possibility of acquiring "distressed assets" led to the creation of a number of private equity funds looking for such opportunities.

title: Seasons Greetings!
summary: Bank lending is not expected to return in earnest during 2010 and shipping finance will be forced to continue adapting to difficult conditions. Nevertheless, there is reason to hope the worst is behind us.

title: The Roaring 00's
summary: As a painful year draws to a close, it is worth remembering that the end of 2009 also caps off what is likely to be remembered as one of the strongest decades in the history of the tanker market. For much of the past ten years, industry participants have seen the visibility of tankers rise as demand growth in developing markets sent them to ever‐more distant shores.

title: AG ‐ FE (260kt)
summary: 1YR TC 3YR TC The enormous gap between the spot market's average and top earnings helped attract new sources of capital into the industry. The heightened profile of tankers was reflected in a frenzy of shipping‐related IPOs and a series of newbuilding orders placed with an expectation of selling the delivered vessel for profit.

title: Demand Develops
summary: That bull market was spurred largely by rapidly expanding crude oil and refined product demand in the developing world. As shown in the chart below, Chinese demand growth played a particularly important role in sustaining the growth of overall crude oil and refined product demand over the decade.

title: China
summary: Other World While demand growth began to weaken in the United States and other demand centers after 2005, consistent demand increases from China placed it squarely at the center of the market's focus during the second half of the decade. This dynamic has only strengthened in the wake of the economic crisis, which presented China with opportunities to secure its future supply at reduced prices.

title: Cyclical Thinking
summary: The current state of the tanker market reflects wider conditions of the international economy just as the explosive growth experienced earlier in the decade was a product of expansionary forces that prevailed at the time. While few would understate the seriousness of the challenges currently facing the tanker market, it can be argued that the state of despair is heightened when those challenges are viewed from the perspective of the market highs experienced in the middle years of the 2000s.

title: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
section_path: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
section_path_text: The Down and Dirty: 2009's Top Charterers
summary: With refinery utilizations low and volumes on long‐haul trade routes sapped by a 2 million barrel per day drop in worldwide demand, it comes as no surprise that 2009 saw a marked slowdown of activity in the tanker market. The recently completed year was one in which the tanker market was beset by forces both specific to the industry and completely out of its control.

title: Chart: 2009 - Top Dirty Charterers - What a Difference a Year Makes!
section_path: Chart: 2009 - Top Dirty Charterers - What a Difference a Year Makes!

summary: In terms of total fixtures across vessel classes, Shell maintained its position as top charterer in 2009, with five more reported fixtures than in 2008, for a total of 691. As shown, the top ten overall charterers have remained essentially the same group over the past two years, while some jockeying for position among them led to minor changes this year.

title: 2009 - Top 10 VLCC Charterers
summary: The fact that all but two of the top ten VLCC charterers for 2009 are Asian based companies speaks to the central role that developing nations of that region have played in supporting ton‐mile demand this year. The reduction of westward bound fixtures from the Arabian Gulf explains the reduced position of ExxonMobil and Shell as well as the exit of BP and Chevron from the top ten this year.

title: 2009 - Top 10 Suezmax Charterers
summary: Suezmaxes sustained a 15 percent drop in reported spot market activity from 2008 levels last year. Among top ten Suezmax charterers, CSSA and Shell swapped the first and third positions on the list from their positions on last year, while Sun moved from the fourth to the second most active on the list, with nine less fixtures.

title: 2009 - Top 10 Aframax Charterers
summary: A review of reported spot fixtures reveals a three percent reduction in activity on Aframax tankers in 2009. Shell maintained its position as top charter of Aframax vessels in 2009, and as has been the case in years past, the top ten charterers remained the same, although there were some changes in their relative positions.

title: 2009 - Top 10 Panamax Charterers
summary: The only market segment to see an increase in activity last year, Panamax fixtures grew slightly from 944 in 2008 to 958 last year and saw more changes in the top ten than other market segments. While Valero, Citgo, and Trafigura, respectively 5 th , 8 th , and 9 th on last year's list, dropped from the top ten in 2009, Vitol, Hess and PMI replaced them in the ranks of top Panamax charterers last year.

title: PMI
summary: While reported spot market activity presents only a portion of total fixture volume, this overview of 2009 spot market activity conforms to the dominant narratives of the tanker market over the past year. The continually rising profile of Asian charterers revealed in the lists above is a natural extension of the strength of demand growth displayed in emerging eastern markets last year.

title: Holy 2010!
summary: Just when it seemed like the tanker market was poised to hobble along for another year, spot market freight rates have again surprised everyone. Freezing temperatures across Asia, Europe and the United States helped set off a rally in tanker markets this week.

title: Chart: VLCC Spot Earnings Vs. Arabian Gulf Availabilities

title: AG ‐ FE (260kt)
summary: VLCCs Next 30 Days VLCC Next 30 Days ‐ 2009 Average VLCC Next 30 Days ‐ 2010 YTD For much of last year's fourth quarter, the tanker market was in the doldrums, with rates stagnating on low crude oil demand. At least part of the movement in tanker markets this week can be attributed to the end of the holiday season, with more market activity creating opportunities to bid up rates for ships in position to make laydays.

title: Let it Snow!
summary: The seasonal increase in activity has been important, but inclement weather has emerged as the main driver of the recent strength in the tanker market. Tankers plying through seasonal rough seas and reduced daylight hours, especially those attempting to traverse ice‐clogged waterways, are more likely to encounter delays.

title: East Meets West
summary: While fixtures headed east in advance of the upcoming Chinese New Year have played an role in driving the rate spike, there are also some positive signs for Western demand within the recent resurgence of spot market rates. The volume of VLCC liftings from the Arabian Gulf are currently at 94 for January, above the one‐year average of 89 liftings per month but slightly below the number of liftings seen in January 2009.

title: West
summary: East West % Total Expect cargoes to be competing for ships over the next few weeks as fewer than 50 VLCCs are available in the Arabian Gulf over the next 30 days, with as many as 90 cargoes likely. The run‐up in reported spot market rates will likely result in buyers, sellers, and charterers all re‐evaluating their next moves.

title: Clean Sweepers: 2009's Top Clean Charterers
summary: Reported spot fixture activity in 2009 for clean petroleum products picked up noticeably over the level seen in 2008. Between these years, market activity captured by reported spot fixtures rose from 2008's level of 4,913 by nearly 16 percent.

title: Turnover at the Top
summary: Shell returned yet again last year to claim the top slot (a position they also held as 2009's dirty spot market top charterer). Some 90 percent of 2008's top ten active charterers returned in 2009, but most saw their relative rankings rearranged.

title: Suezmax (120,000 - 199,999 DWT)
summary: Spot market fixtures of Suezmaxes were noted in 2009, while none were reported in 2008. Activity by Vitol, Koch, Morgan Stanley, ST Shipping and other companies contributed to this sector's 10 reported spot fixtures.

title: Aframax ‐ LR2 (80,000 - 119,999 DWT)
summary: Activity in 2009's Aframax (LR2) market was similar to that of 2008. From a level of 456 reported spot fixtures in 2008, activity noted in 2009 rose by just four fixtures.

title: YNCC
summary: The predominant clean trade for Aframaxes continues to be the Arabian Gulf - Far East naphtha trade for petrochemicals with nearly 31 percent of total fixture activity.

title: Panamax ‐ LR1 (60,000 - 79,999 DWT)
summary: Panamax last year grew by 187 reported spot fixture activity - or nearly 33 percent - over 2008's level of 578. As with the Aframax sector, both Shell and Vitol returned in 2009 as the top two Panamax (LR1) charterers.

title: Handymax (37,500 - 59,999 DWT)
summary: Overall reported clean Handymax spot market activity was up nearly 22 percent from 2008. Vitol trumped Shell for the top Handymax slot in 2009.

title: Small (25,000 - 37,499 DWT)
summary: Litasco retained the slot of top charterer in the Small vessel sector during 2009. Clearlake moved from fifth position in 2008 to 2009's second slot.

title: What's Ahead for 2010?
summary: Restoration of economic health during 2010 seems likely to unfurl unevenly throughout the world. As some economies - notably those of China and India - sprint ahead of the rest of the world's countries, clean petroleum product trade routes could likely change as supply chases emerging pockets of unfulfilled local demand.

title: In Like A Tiger...
summary: In the opening of 2010, the freight market has acted like a tiger as the freight rates have surged across the board. Just a year ago, market fundamentals seemed far bleaker while tanker freight rates were hanging on, waiting for the proverbial "other shoe to drop." A year ago, Poten & Partners conducted an open survey on the tanker and oil markets ( In the Year of the Ox , January 23, 2009) to gather popular opinions on the upcoming year.

title: Economics and Banking
summary: The vast majority of replies to the survey believed that a recovery in the US economy would take a year or more, with 46% believing economic improvement would take a year and 32% thinking it would take at least two. Economic improvement can hinge on many factors, but by using the Dow Jones Industrial average as one initial indicator of confidence there has been some improvement.

title: Crude Oil Demand and Price
summary: When polled about expectations on whether crude oil demand would remain flat, increase or decrease, respondents were evenly divided amongst the three. Based on the latest market report, the year‐on‐year increase in first quarter 2010 worldwide crude oil consumption is estimated to be 1.65 million barrels per day, or about 2%, according to the IEA.

title: Major Mergers and Freight Rates
summary: When asked whether VLCC freight rates would average $75,000 per day, $50,000 per day or $20,000 per day, 73% of people replied $50,000 per day. The chart below shows the spot market rates for Arabian Gulf to Far East and the US Gulf.

title: 73% Answered
summary: When asked about whether the first merger would take place amongst tanker companies or major oil companies, 66% of people expected tanker companies to converge. Although many expected consolidation in 2009, the market did not produce any major mergers.

title: Asset Prices and Newbuildings
summary: The relative values in the asset markets have continued to leave many waiting for the flurry of activity on the back of strained financial conditions within companies. While the secondhand sale and purchase market seems to have seen its share of transactions, the newbuilding market has continued to remain quiet, with the notable exception of a few national oil company orders having been placed.

title: ...Out like a lamb?
summary: With some of the expected events having yet‐to‐materialize by the end of 2009, does that mean 2010 is poised for some shakeups? Perhaps the short‐term upward price pressure on assets will convince the market that the bottom has passed, spurring some interest in shipping assets, or companies on the whole, and also create some opportunities for mergers, acquisitions or newbuilding orders.

title: Cleaning Upwards for a Decade
summary: At the turn of the millennium, India's crude oil refinery capacity stood at just over 1 mbd, and was a net importer of clean petroleum products. Now, following a decade of aggressive growth, India is seated within the top five countries in terms of refinery capacity and is a net exporter of refined petroleum products.
