title: More Ton‐miles on the Horizon?
summary: If the crude oil continues to be sourced from the same regions as 2009, an increase of 1.3 mbd in India's refining capacity would create an incremental increase of roughly 40% or 7 more VLCCs by 2013. However, if the load ratios change over the next four years such that West Africa and the Caribbean offset cargoes from the Arabian Gulf, the incremental demand for VLCCs could have more striking growth.

title: The Storage Story
summary: Use of tankers as floating storage has seemed to consistently capture the attention of those in the tanker and broader oil markets for over a year. In the early part of 2009, crude oil tankers were the bearers of most of the storage activity, but as the year continued clean product tankers made a significant emergence into such employment.

title: Clean Storage
summary: Dirty Storage In January, freezing temperatures across North America, Europe and Asia gave a boost to distillate demand. At the same time, spot freight rates for clean product tankers began to rise, creating short‐lived optimism among ship owners that may have otherwise renewed storage charters.

title: US Distillate Demand
summary: AG ‐ FE (75kt) AG ‐ FE (55kt) The release of some vessels back into the spot market seemed to be enough to negatively impact the supply‐demand balance. Perhaps hopeful for a sustained recovery in tanker demand, shipowners opportunistically decided to take their chances in the spot market.

title: Still room to contango
summary: Although the spread between spot and future prices for distillate has narrowed significantly, opportunities will likely persist for traders and shipowners interested in storage plays. This current narrowing can be seen as the result of the uptick in near‐term demand for product, but material recovery in worldwide demand for industrial, heating and transportation fuels will be required in order to change the structure of the curve toward backwardation on a more permanent basis.

title: China's Bright Horizon
summary: China's growing reliance on seaborne crude oil imports will set the tone of the tanker market for the coming decade. As shown in the chart below, the size of China's reported spot program has increased five‐fold over the past ten years; rising from an equivalent of 11 VLCCs in 2000 to one of more than 55 VLCCs last year.

title: Arabian Gulf
summary: Caribbean Mediterranean Red Sea UK Cont. West Africa In reality, Chinese requirements for petroleum transportation are significantly larger than reflected above.

title: The Arabian Gulf and Beyond
summary: Second only to the United States in oil consumption, demand for transportation fuels from China's growing middle class has been a factor in worldwide crude oil demand for years. The International Energy Agency expects China's oil demand to continue expanding at a rate of 4.7% in 2010, reaching 8.9 million barrels per day.

title: Refining its Role
summary: Also likely to impact future trade routes are the Chinese government's efforts to discourage the import of refined petroleum products, most prominently by supporting rapid growth in China's domestic refining sector. The construction of large, complex refineries within China, some built in cooperation with foreign multinationals, has helped expand Chinese crude oil demand in recent years and this trend is expected to continue, as shown in the chart below.

title: Chart: Refinery Capacity Outlook ‐ China
summary: The stockpiling of crude oil and refined products in China has also played a role in supplying demand for ships throughout the market slowdown last year. While changes in Chinese inventories are thought to have contributed significantly to recent Chinese consumption, there remains a great deal of uncertainty regarding inventory practices in China.

title: The Expanding Chinese Fleet
summary: China's expanding middle class, strategic stockpiling, and complex refining capacity ensure that it will continue to be a large ship, crude oil story. Recent efforts to expand ship‐owning may ultimately lead to structural changes in the tanker market.

title: Kuwait Bucks Peak Oil
summary: The combined effect of a weaker oil price environment and the overall decline in worldwide oil consumption has created challenges for those involved in upstream oil resource development. While it is held by some people that most conventional oil reserves have largely been discovered, unconventional sources are receiving increased attention.

title: Going Up!
summary: Kuwaiti production recovered then rose dramatically following the 1991 Gulf war, as can be seen in the chart below, sustaining production in excess of 2.5 million barrels per day (mbd) for the past five years. Kuwait has recently re‐committed itself to a significant increase in production rates during the coming years.

title: Kuwaiti Oil Production & Consumption
summary: While Kuwait has reevaluated some of its expansion plans following the economic downturn, the Kuwaiti Parliament recently approved a plan that will see the nation attempt to raise its production capacity from current levels of around 3.1 mbd to 3.5 mbd over the next five years. Additionally, Kuwait plans to increase total capacity to levels of between 4‐5 mbd by in the years to follow.

title: O PEC - ing Away
summary: When the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meets next week in Vienna, they will help formulate a consensus about the future of global economic recovery. Recent weeks have brought some varied, but generally positive signals of economic recovery in the US while crude oil prices have remained near the range identified as "fair" by some of OPEC's most influential voices.

title: Greater Expectations
summary: OPEC expects worldwide demand to grow by 1.1% this year, reaching 86.6 million barrels per day by the fourth quarter to average 85.24 million barrels per day for the year, as shown in the chart below. Repeating what has become a recurring mantra among forecasters of oil demand, OPEC highlighted that this demand growth is expected to be the result of expanding consumption in countries outside the OECD, especially India and China.

title: Compliance: The Key
summary: Despite these inklings of economic recovery, one reason why OPEC may choose not to make any changes to stated production levels next week is the fact that some of its members are already exceeding the limits already in place. After maintaining historically high levels of compliance to production quotas introduced last year, recent months have seen this compliance slip.

title: No More Fueling Around
summary: When the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) discusses options for regulating marine emissions of greenhouse gases next week, it will make its case that a single standard is preferable to a patchwork of varying fuel requirements. Whatever plan the IMO eventually produces will join an already‐crowded regime of separate marine fuel regulation that has started to become a more prominent feature in the day‐to‐day tanker market.

title: The New Rules
summary: Since January 1 st 2010, vessels docked in European Union ports for more than two hours while not hooked into shore‐side power have been required to use marine gasoil with no more than 0.1% sulfur to power auxiliary equipment. This requirement is the result of an EU directive published back in 2005, one of several marine fuel regulations to come into force in recent years, summarized in the table below.

title: ...More to Come?
summary: The EU's new restrictions on marine fuel burned in port and their effect on spot market rates demonstrate that inconsistent enforcement of regulations can have a significant effect on the bottom line. The rules now being more strictly enforced on a selective basis have been known since 2005, allowing plenty of time for ship owners to meet the new regulations.

title: Capitalizing Together
summary: Capitalizing Together 4 th Annual Capital Link Forum The buzz of finance in shipping returned to the Metropolitan Club in New York City this past Thursday as Capital Link hosted the 4th annual Invest in International Shipping forum. The single day event included a sea of shipowners, finance houses, bankers and market analysts all of whom contributed via panels and general market discussions.

title: Chart: PTI vs Equity Index
summary: The PTI is up 72 points or over 250% since the end of August 2009, following a brisk start to tanker markets in the beginning of the year, signaling signs of a recovering freight market.

title: The Tanker Romp
summary: The afternoon was a tanker filled romp with panelists reaching across both the crude oil and refined product tanker vessel sectors. Fotis Giannakoulis, VP of Research at Morgan Stanley moderated the crude oil tanker panel which consisted of Mr.

title: Supply Story
summary: In addition to speaking on behalf of their respective tanker trades, there was much discussion in regards to the elephant looming in the back of the room - newbuild orders. While last year's tanker panel focused primarily on long‐term charter coverage, this year focused quite a bit on supply as shipowners pointed out that there are still a vast amount of ships scheduled to be delivered in the coming years, especially as 2009 encountered "slippage" or delays in both the crude oil and product tanker sectors.

title: Drill, Baby, Drill?
summary: Yes, but this time it's not Sarah Palin. In what feels like a sharp contrast to his pre‐election mantra, this week saw President Obama announce an end to the prohibition on oil and gas exploration in selected coastal areas of the United States.

title: Same as the Old Boss?
summary: In 2008, Congress allowed a decades‐old ban on offshore domestic drilling to expire. The President's announcement this week effectively served to revive an effort spearheaded by the Bush Administration following the end of the drilling moratorium.

title: True Impact to Come
summary: Exploration and development of oil and gas resources in the regions opened by Obama's announcement, contingent as they are on environmental assessments and local approvals, will likely take years to materialize. Offshore reserves are currently estimated to hold between 39 and 62 billion barrels of oil and between 168 and 294 trillion feet of natural gas.

title: A Step Forward
summary: Aside from a desire to create desperately needed jobs, Obama's belated embrace of offshore drilling is partially intended to win the support of Republicans and reluctant Democrats for broader energy legislation. A version of the energy bill passed the House last year before stalling in the Senate, where a new compromise version is expected to be considered in coming weeks.

title: Volumes Return
summary: The recent strength in VLCC earnings has been propelled mostly by an increase in overall fixture activity and signals of strengthening demand for crude oil and refined products. Less dramatic than the rally which inaugurated 2010, improving conditions for VLCCs have nonetheless provided the market with a degree of optimism as it enters the second quarter, a period which usually witnesses a softening of freight rates.

title: West
summary: East West % Total Also significant for the progress of the overall economic recovery are increases in the percentage of West‐bound liftings from the Arabian Gulf. 16% of reported April VLCC cargoes leaving the Arabian Gulf are destined for markets in the West, the second consecutive monthly increase in the Western portion of such liftings.

title: Looking Up
summary: Indications of increasing fixture activity out of the Arabian Gulf join a series of positive indicators for both the domestic and international economies. The US Commerce Department recently reported that the domestic economy grew at a rate of 5.6% in the fourth quarter of 2009, its fastest pace in six years.

title: Strait Flush
summary: As a bunkering port near the Arabian Gulf, Fujairah already plays an important role in international tanker markets. It has long served an anchorage point for ships awaiting nomination for cargoes in the Arabian Gulf, but coming years are likely to see Fujairah's role expand.

title: Bypassing a Strait
summary: The diverted marine traffic the ADCOP pipeline is expected to bring to Fujairah has inspired a significant expansion of terminal facilities there. The deepwater port at Fujairah, which has already seen a steady increase in shipping traffic over recent years, will reportedly be outfitted with a number of loading facilities capable of receiving vessels with deadweights up to 180,000 dwt.

title: Post Volcanic Ash Syndrome
summary: As market dynamics unleashed along with columns of smoke and ash from the Eyjafjallajokull volcano continue to work their way through the international economy, the full effect of the week's events has yet to fully reveal itself. It is already clear that the cessation of airplane traffic across Europe sharply reduced demand for jet fuel in the region, with consequences that filtered through crude oil and refined product markets this week.

title: $ / mt
summary: Jet fuel cargoes are often delivered to pipelines that carry supplies directly to airports and storage at these sites tends to be limited. With flights grounded and little additional onshore storage available, the logistics of delivering jet fuel to customers in Northwest Europe were severely complicated, prompting some airlines to declare force majeure and stop accepting delivery.

title: "Majeure" Challenges
summary: With some of the fuel's main customers unable to accept delivery, European refiners must confront the challenge of what to do with jet fuel supplies intended for the continent's cancelled flights. Area refiners producing unneeded kerosene have two main options: they can blend the excess fuel into middle distillates or change their configurations to reduce jet fuel production.

title: Floating Inquiries
summary: A contango pricing structure in European jet fuel to gasoil swap markets was widened by the sharp drop in near‐term jet fuel demand following the flight stoppage. The premium for jet fuel in Northwest Europe over gasoil futures on the ICE exchange narrowed from $45 per metric ton on April 15 to $35 per metric ton on April 19, as shown in the following chart.

title: Tankers Awaiting
summary: Going forward, unwinding the logjam surrounding delivery of jet fuel to airports in Europe is likely to keep ships out of the market and could lend some support to clean carrier freight rates. Some increase in floating storage fixtures as a result of opportunities created by the jet fuel demand disruptions in Europe this week is likely, though which cargoes are most likely to be stored on those fixtures depends mostly on what regional refiners choose to do with their jet fuel.

title: Tarred and Feathered Etouffee
summary: The oil spill which began with an explosion on an oil rig in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico has developed into a rapidly‐deteriorating situation threatening local wildlife and national commerce and is also likely to have longer‐term implications for recently‐announced plans to increase offshore drilling.

title: Location, Location, Location
summary: The volumes of crude oil gushing from the well have inspired widespread comparisons to the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska, but its location dictates that this spill will have a more significant impact on the spot tanker market. The map below shows the location and distribution of other oil spills that shaped regulation and reputations in oil and tanker industries.

title: Historical Oil Spills
summary: While the Exxon Valdez spill complicated operations at just one distant port, the Deepwater Horizon spill is occurring in a heavily‐trafficked area responsible for about 30 percent of US domestic oil production. Ships have been instructed to avoid contact with the heavy black floating oil at all costs and maintain a safe speed while moving through lighter oil on the surface when forced to traverse affected areas.

title: Let the Finger Pointing Begin!
summary: The effort to stop the gushing oil well 5,000 feet below sea level in the Gulf of Mexico has moved into a critical next stage with the arrival of a four‐story containment dome designed to capture the oil at the site. The 100‐ton concrete and steel dome is being guided by cameras as robots lower it directly above the well currently spewing oil into the U.S.

title: Managing Expectations
summary: Despite the expectations of many, the Deepwater Horizon spill has, to date, had only a moderate impact on freight rates in the tanker market. Specially‐crafted clauses have been inserted into charterparties for voyages through the area, as owners naturally seek a premium for taking the risks associated with bringing their vessels into the US Gulf.

title: Slowing Momentum
summary: The clearest indication of the spill's immediate impact is the 30‐day moratorium on new exploration licenses announced by President Obama almost immediately following the accident. It is highly likely that the spill will delay those efforts for far longer than 30 days as it will take years for all of the investigations likely to stem from the incident to run their course.

title: Undiscovered Resources
summary: Coming on the heels of a rhetorical embrace of the role of domestic oil and gas production in meeting America's long‐term energy goals by the Obama Administration, the Deepwater Horizon spill could not have come at a worse time for U.S. On the bright side for tanker owners nervously watching developments from the sidelines: it looks like we will continue to be import‐bound for at least the time being.

title: It's All Greek to Me
summary: As Greece's debt problems have blossomed from a national concern into a near existential threat to the European monetary union, and even beyond, the particulars of its economy and culture have come under harsh scrutiny. Likely facing a future of economic challenges and regulatory adjustments, Greece has an important asset in its storied shipping industry.

title: Back in the Saddle
summary: Financial trouble at home has not slowed Greek activity in the sale and purchase market this year, which has been particularly active after a lull during 2009's down market. Public and private Greek companies have reportedly both been among the most active in placing orders at Far Eastern shipyards this year.

title: Greek Shipping Orderbook ‐ Tankers
summary: While family money has been the traditional means by which Greek companies established their shipping presence, they have also led the way in public finance for the shipping sector. Of the 34 shipping companies across sectors to go public between 2005 and 2009, 20 were Greek.

title: Far Eastern Exports?
summary: A surge in production coinciding with Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) cuts allowed Russia to briefly assume the role of the world's largest crude oil exporter in 2009. Russia has maintained high levels of crude oil production this year, but it is the country's expanding export infrastructure that has been felt most directly within the tanker market.

title: Mongolia
summary: The Kozmino Oil Port has a 21 meter depth and can accommodate tankers with deadweights between 80,000 and 150,000 dwt. The standard cargo size from Kozmino is about 100,000 mt and since the port's opening, cargoes have overwhelmingly been carried on Aframax tankers.

title: Jan ‐ 10
summary: Feb‐10 Mar ‐ 10 Apr ‐ 10 May‐10 TD More than half of reported spot fixtures from Kozmino have gone to South Korea, with Japan and the West Coast of the United States as the next most frequent destinations reported for these cargoes. Smaller percentages of ex‐Kozmino fixtures have reportedly been exported to China, Thailand, Taiwan and elsewhere in region.

title: Driving Towards Normality
summary: The American summer driving season that typically kicks off with Memorial Day weekend is a period when oil and tanker markets traditionally anticipate an uptick in refined product demand. For each of the past two years, however, the durability of this seasonal demand surge has been tested by extraordinary conditions in oil markets driven largely by conditions in the economy.

title: Priced to Move
summary: Pressured by the European debt crisis, a strengthening dollar and various geopolitical concerns, recent weeks have seen the price of crude oil drop sharply; from an average of about $84 per barrel in April to the current level of $74.55 per barrel. The Energy Information Administration (EIA), reports that April witnessed a stabilization and modest turnaround in gasoline consumption in the United States.

title: Premium
summary: Regular Current Price Premium Current Price Regular Whether incremental demand is met by imports or higher output from domestic refineries is generally determined by a delicate equilibrium between freight rates and refinery utilization. In years past, the seasonal uptick in refined product demand that accompanies summer driving season could be relied on to lend some support to freight rates for clean tankers.

title: Drilling Deep?
summary: While it has been evident for weeks that the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is a transformative event for the entire energy industry, a widespread sense of confusion following the announcement of a six‐month moratorium on deepwater drilling in the Gulf of Mexico leaves its near‐term impact largely unclear. If, as some fear, the moratorium drags on past the current six‐ month timeframe, it could exacerbate the United States' long‐term dependence on imported oil and have potentially significant consequences for the development of regional tanker trade flows.

title: Confusion Reigns
summary: The sense of uncertainty which has greeted the announcement of the moratorium reflects the likelihood that attempts to "pause" deepwater operations in the Gulf for six months could result in longer delays. Waiting for a report and list of recommendations by a commission appointed by the President could prolong the ban, especially as the political storm surrounding the spill continues to build as mid‐term elections approach.

title: $ per barrel
summary: These developments all threaten to undermine a plan to use domestic drilling to help mitigate dependence on foreign oil announced by the President in March. Deepwater production was an important piece of that plan and an extended delay could result in as much as 400 kb/d in reduced domestic production, according to the American Petroleum Institute.

title: Taking the Long View
summary: As the company deals with an array of short‐term challenges related to the disastrous oil spill in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, BP briefly turned its attention to the long‐term this week with the release of its annual Statistical Review.

title: US: Leading Non‐ OPEC Growth
summary: BP sees global oil consumption as having fallen some 1.2 million barrels per day last year, which is also the largest fall since 1982. Drops in oil demand were not consistent across regions, though, with OECD demand displaying the sharpest decline on record while oil demand in non‐ OECD countries continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace.

title: Thousand Barrels Per Day
summary: Last year's plunging demand for oil helped to make it a landmark year which many in the energy and tanker markets would like to forget. Although many of the figures related in this year's Statistical Review serve to remind just how challenging conditions have become, they also contain important reminders of long‐established trends that will support oil and tanker markets in the future.

title: Sustainable Demand
summary: The rally which has brought VLCC earnings on the Arabian Gulf - Far East voyage to a five month high has been driven by the continued strength in Eastern demand and improving sentiment across markets. Although short‐term tonnage supply in the Arabian Gulf is starting to catch up with demand, positive sentiment mounts for large ship sectors on a fundamental level.

title: Rippling Effects
summary: Inquiries for east‐bound fixing activity have reportedly been a bit quiet this week due to the Dragon Boat Festival in Taiwan and China. In advance of the holiday, however, an overnight surge in third‐decade June fixtures by Chinese charterers forced owners to recalculate their freight rate ideas.

title: Further on the Road
summary: While the rhythms of the Chinese market may have provided the immediate push, an improving demand picture in Western markets has also contributed to recent strengthening in rates. An increase in gasoline demand reported by the Energy Information Administration earlier this week supported the positive sentiment about demand recovery.

title: Looking Ahead?
summary: It is interesting to note rumblings that charterers already actively pursuing tonnage with fixing dates later than mid‐July have played a role in driving recent activity levels. This suggests a sentiment, at least among some, that recent strength in earnings will continue.

title: Public Displays
summary: As difficult as it was to see the light just a year ago, optimism in the tanker market has been the flavor of the month. Despite European debt worries and oil spill anxiety stateside, generally healthy freight rates and moderated fleet growth have let shipping companies enjoy the freight rate spoils over the last couple of weeks.

title: Challenges Continue
summary: Despite apparent optimism about the tanker market's future, lingering uncertainties in the wider international economy have closed the window for new initial public offerings (IPO) at present. On the back of the shipping boom during 2004 to 2008, publically‐listed shipping companies gained street credibility and general popularity among retail investors.

title: IPOs
summary: Follow‐on Offerings The role of public money has brought to light an apparent disconnect between asset prices and freight rates. As asset prices edge somewhat higher, pressures on freight rates are likely to follow.

title: Harbinger Wind?
summary: After threatening to follow a path that some projections showed would send it through the heart of the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, Hurricane Alex weakened into a topical depression which broke up over central Mexico this week.

title: Closures & Outages
summary: While Hurricane Alex did not come into direct contact with the main oil spill region, the storm did force closures of important oil loading ports and production sites this week. The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port was forced to halt offloading operations on June 29 and two of Mexico's main oil ports on the Gulf Coast were also forced to briefly close.

title: Offshore Field Production
summary: This storm also offered a preview of the challenges future storms might pose to clean‐up and recovery efforts in the U.S. Hurricane Alex's fierce winds brought oil‐filled waves to area beaches and raised fears that more oil would be brought into local wetlands.

title: Unwinding Subsidies
summary: Alongside China, India has emerged as an important driver of many of the trends expected to determine the direction of future oil and tanker markets. Its rapidly‐growing economy has been important in shifting the center of oil demand growth eastward.

title: Diversification to Follow?
summary: One of the most important motivations for the liberalization of gasoline prices in India has been a desire to minimize the economic effects of government subsidies in light of India's recent demand growth. While the Finance Ministry acknowledged that the removal of subsidies would likely bring about an increase in inflation in the near term, the change is also expected to help reduce India's $5.5 billion oil subsidy bill.

title: AG
summary: CAR MED RS SEA WAF Government subsidies are intended to ensure that the poor have adequate access to fuel supplies, and the debate about subsidies reform in India has been a long and heated one. A previous attempt to remove subsidies in 2002 was derailed when it was ensnarled in election‐ year politics and the recent announcement has also been met with protest marches and strikes.

title: Sanctions Gain Teeth
summary: With the enactment of a new U.S. sanctions regime earlier this month, the tanker industry has once again found itself drawn directly into the fray surrounding Iran.

title: Targeting Tankers
summary: An exception for underwriters and insurance providers who have practiced due diligence in establishing procedures to comply with the prohibition was included in the law. Ongoing efforts to isolate Tehran are, nonetheless, having an effect on the ability to secure insurance for refined product imports into Iran.

title: Trade Flows Frozen?
summary: A Government Accountability Office report earlier this year named companies actively involved in trading gasoline into Iran and subsequent pressure on these companies forced most to relent and end their supply contracts. Throughout 2010, they have been joined by a procession of companies including Eni, Total, and Reliance which have announced that they would end business dealings with Iran.

title: 2010 YTD
summary: Negotiations to reconcile different versions of the sanctions bill reportedly focused on the need for flexibility in light of the effort to gather support for United Nations sanctions against Iran. To help provide this flexibility, the law allows for a one‐year waiver for companies found in violation that are closely cooperating with multilateral efforts against Iran.

title: Making Virtual A Reality
summary: Facing a likely future of tightened environmental regulation and rising marine fuel costs, efforts are underway to standardize efficiency practices in the tanker industry. Chief among these efforts is the "Virtual Arrival" scheme developed by Intertanko and the Oil Companies International Marine Forum (OCIMF).

title: Not - So - Slow!
summary: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) working group to promote the idea has recognized that for it to be successful it must be accepted by all involved parties. Attempts to introduce the Virtual Arrival clause into charterparties have received a mostly luke‐warm reception thus far.

These assessors must then be trusted to provide an auditable post‐voyage record in compliance with all legal requirements.

title: Preparing to Measure Emissions
summary: Despite the failure of UN Climate Change negotiators in Copenhagen to incorporate shipping into their final Accord last year, there is a suspicion among some that regulation of maritime emissions of greenhouse gases at some level is inevitable. In March, the Marine Environmental Protection Committee (MEPC) of the IMO met in London to discuss competing proposals for market‐based measures to regulate marine emissions of greenhouse gases.

title: The Asset Game
summary: One can't help but notice a disconnect between slipping freight rates, weak demand fundamentals and the surge of newbuilding tanker orders seen in recent months. Asset values are derived from the expected earning of that asset over its life, but with the tanker market sending mixed signals on the pace of recovery, other forces are ostensibly in play.

title: VLCC Newbuilding Price
summary: AG ‐ FE (260kt) Over the past two years, a lack of liquidity in both financing ability and the amount of deal flow left a tanker asset market that was largely untested. Not surprisingly, the credit crunch was largely responsible for this turn of events.

title: New Orders ‐ China
summary: New Orders ‐ Korea Secondhand:Newbuilding The reason for the heightened interest in newbuildings is likely two fold. Forward delivery allows shipowners to enter the market with a brand new asset at some point in the future, hopefully during the demand recovery.

title: Perception & Reality
summary: For better or worse, expectations, momentum, and emotion are factors that can significantly impact shipowners' decision making. Although more intangible than raw materials costs, these perceived drivers can have a substantial impact and can trigger a run‐up in prices quite easily.

title: New Study: China: Driving Global Commerce and Tanker Trade

While owners of older model vehicles and other internal combustion engines might harbor concerns that use of E15 gasoline might transform their prized possessions into roadside trash, the EPA does not.

summary: In this week's Petroleum Status Report, the US Energy Intelligence Agency (EIA) reported that US commercial crude inventories rose a higher-than-expected 3.7 MB last week, to 379.5 MB, the highest level since 1990. Crude oil prices declined on the news, also confronted by electoral uncertainty and recessionary conditions in Europe and weaker Chinese economic statistics.

title: Capesize
summary: The gloomiest of ends to the year looming large for the big ships with rates dropping sharply in all areas. In the Atlantic, the coal run from Puerto Bolivar to Rotterdam fell to $6.00 for 1-10 January while a 181,000-tonner open Port Talbot fixed for a transatlantic round at $9,500 daily.

title: Panamax
summary: The bull run for Panamaxes particularly in the Atlantic came to a halt as the week drew to a close with owners now seemingly prepared to drop rates substantially to cover the festive period and into the New Year. Some described the cuts as ‘brutal' - today a 2013-built post-Panamax fixing from Gibraltar 26-30 December for two to three laden legs within the Atlantic at $7,500 daily.

title: Supramax
summary: A relatively quiet week with rates improving in the Atlantic and trading slowing down in the Pacific. Period wise, a 63,000-dwt 2015-built was reportedly booked for four to six months at $14,750 per day basis South West Pass delivery.

title: Handysize
summary: This sector has performed better than most this week with some very notable fixtures being concluded as the BHSI reached its highest level of 596 since 7 April 2014 when it touched 588. Going into next week the question was how many ships and requirements remained for 2016.

title: Capesize
summary: Simply not enough cargo to absorb the volume of ships coming onto the market and at best rates were just about flat. Paper values perked up briefly Thursday then settled lower and as October closes out little sign of any fourth quarter cheer.

title: Panamax
summary: Early ships in the East were chasing business with charterers able to in many instances fix on an aps basis. Today there were rumours of an LME open Yosu fixing at $5,000 daily for a NoPac round while some owners headed off in ballast hoping for better luck the closer they to arriving NoPac or were heading off to the US Gulf.

title: Supramax/Handysize
summary: Generally quiet although activity picked up over the course of the week. There were a number of vessels awaiting their Friday fixture.

title: Supramax
summary: The US Gulf appeared the place to be with owners securing better than last done. This included the Soho Merchant 64,000 dwt built 2015 fixed at $14,000 daily for delivery US Gulf for trip Singapore-Japan.

title: Handysize
summary: There remained a continued reluctance from owners, charterers and brokers to divulge reportable fixtures. This week's fixtures included the St Andrew 32,688 dwt delivery dop Cigading for two laden legs redelivery Far East at $6,000 daily.

title: Capesize
summary: Another week of largely flat rates with the odd firmer rate reported. Today the West Australia/China run for 170,000 tonne 10% cargoes hovered around $4.30 to $4.40 for 16-19 February loading dates with now one of the majors reportedly paying $4.75 for a ship to load 11 February.

title: Panamax
summary: Unsettling times for panamax operators with the BDI near historic lows and the BPI continuing to slide. Transatlantic trading remained negligible with charterers able to secure voyage rates at their ideas with little or no negotiation.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: In the Atlantic, with the possible exception of the US Gulf area, it has been another difficult week for the owners. In the US Gulf however, there was at least a glimmer of hope as vessels in early positions were able to achieve somewhat improved levels.

title: Capesize
summary: Capesize rates traded in a narrow range during a week that saw the BDI drop to a record low. At the start there were some minor gains but as the week closed out and the Lunar New Year approached rates came under downward pressure.

title: Panamax
summary: Rates here saw some gains as the week closed out but few were predicting whether this would last. There remained a significant volume of ships but owners were resisting low rates particularly for US Gulf/transatlantic cargoes and fronthaul with some limited gains evident.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: In the Atlantic, another tough week for the owners with a feeling that the slightly better tone in the US Gulf for the early positions was now not so evident. A 2005 built 55,280 dwt unit was reported to have been booked by a grain house for a trip from the US Gulf to Singapore-Japan at about $9,000 daily.

title: Capesize
summary: With various national holidays in Asia the end of the week has been very quiet indeed. During the week the 5 TC average lost about 13% value, more because of weaker Atlantic rates.

title: Panamax
summary: The Atlantic has been slow through the week although there has been trading from South America which continues to take tonnage from the Indian Ocean. A 79,000 dwt in ballast from EC India secured delivery retroactive for a trip via South America redelivery east around $7,000 daily.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Without getting too carried away, there appeared to be one or two rays of light in the North Atlantic, and the market in this area looked to have ‘bottomed out' at least for the time being. A 2004 built 56,000 dwt ‘Mitsui' type was reported to have been fixed for a trip from the US Gulf to Singapore-Japan at a better $11,000 daily.

title: Capesize
summary: A flat market for capesizes, particularly in the East where the rate for cargoes from West Australia to China held around $4.40 for 170,000 tonne cargoes from either Dampier or Port Hedland to Qingdao. BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto and FMG all fixed at these levels with talk that the former paid $4.50 for prompt ship.

title: Panamax
summary: There were some pockets of resistance in the Atlantic with tonnage tighter, but rates remained at very low levels. The US Gulf saw fewer prompt ships but this so far has yet to result in any improvement in rates.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A patchy week, but with better levels of activity in some areas, there was more reason for owners to feel hopeful that the bottom of the market may have been reached. In the North Atlantic, a 2013 built 57,000 dwt ‘Dolphin' type was reported to have been fixed from the US Gulf to Singapore-Japan at around $10,500 daily.

title: Capesize
summary: A good volume of fixing in the East and on one day alone over a dozen ships fixed from west Australia to China, but rates remained locked around $4.50. These levels showed very poor returns on time charter and although owners were prepared to fix voyage business they would not do the equivalent time charter rate.

title: Panamax
summary: Atlantic trading remained very slow with new business this week failing to absorb much of the early tonnage. There was some pressure for charterers with US Gulf cargoes but here too the market now appeared evenly matched.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A more encouraging week for the owners as rates started to improve in most areas. In the US-Gulf a nicely described 2012 built 58,600 dwt unit was booked for a trip to Singapore-Japan at about $13,000 daily or maybe a shade less.

title: VLCCs
summary: The Middle East Gulf continued to weaken with S-Oil fixing 272,000 tonnes to Onsan at WS 49.5 and China discharge went at both WS 52 and 53 level, while Korean discharge is understood to have been covered at WS50.5 and now rumoured a shade less at WS 49. Trips to Thailand and Singapore have been covered at WS 54.5, all basis 270,000 tonnes cargo size.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, a slow start to the week saw rates drift down to WS 85 to Europe and a USAC discharge covered at WS 80. Later in the week as enquiries increased rates jumped from the mid WS 90S to WS 107.5/110.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, levels have remained steady between WS 100/105 cross Med depending on the voyage. Libya has been busier this week with rates here in the low/mid WS 120s but this is not deemed a true reflection of the market.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to US Gulf has been a story of fixing and failing with tonnage still open Mid March and levels remain unchanged at around WS 125 for 55,000 tonnes to US Gulf.

title: Clean
summary: The market saw a high of WS 187.5 for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC. Thereafter a build up of tonnage and slow down in enquiry has seen rates come off, with the last reported here now at WS 160.

title: Capesize
summary: The BCI fell to new lows this week with one of the longest periods of weak rates seen in many years. Some owners now have ships in ‘soft' lay up, but operators need to keep vessels moving and chased business.

title: Panamax
summary: The focus here remained on South America and it appeared that the rates were slowly improving even for March ships. A kamsarmax (coming from India) with Recalada delivery 25 March agreed $11,750 daily plus a $175,000 bonus for a trip to the East - a rate that was not on the table at the beginning of the week.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Handysizes in the US Gulf remain tight and appear to be enjoying better times: a three year old 35,000 tonner obtained $11,000 daily for a trip from the Gulf to west coast South America. A 37,000 tonner was trading a trip to the Black Sea around $10,000 daily, with unconfirmed talk higher rates had been seen for similar trips.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, the market has been steady this week. The rate for 270,000 tonnes initially dipped to WS 49 for South Korea discharge, but thereafter levels remained largely unchanged.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates initially eased as charterers held back. The market fell to the mid WS 90s early in the week, but a rush of early April cargoes combined with a finely balanced tonnage list saw rates recover.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, the market softened during the week as a healthy tonnage list combined with minimal Turkish straits delays and a lack of enquiry saw rates fall to WS100 for conventional voyages. Libya loaders continued to pay a premium of around 7.5/10 points more.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to US Gulf remained unchanged at around WS 125 for 55,000 tonnes to US Gulf. The panamax market in the Caribbean dropped sharply to WS 150 and brokers said rates here may drop further with ballasters adding to the competition.

title: Clean
summary: The market for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC initially slipped to WS 152.5 but the market rallied mid-week to WS 160 as strong enquiry thinned out tonnage list. A replacement cargo was subsequently covered at WS185 which appeared to be the catalyst for owners and this number has now been repeated for a ‘normal position'.

title: Capesize
summary: Still a largely depressing week for the big ships although there was an increase in rates from West Australia to China for late March but this was largely the result of draft issues at Dampier prompting a premium. Rio Tinto conceded $4.70 for a 28 March onwards 170,000 tonne 10% cargo from Dampier to Qingdao and the charterer reportedly remained in the market.

title: Panamax
summary: South American activity drove the market this week with active fixing and improvement in rates for cargoes to the East. A 74,000 tonner 2000-built reportedly agreed $12,000 daily plus a $200,000 bonus for 9-14 April from east coast South America to the East.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: More activity in the Atlantic especially in the southern hemisphere as owners started to feel more optimistic. A 2005 built 52,400 dwt ‘Tess 52' type was reported to have been booked delivery Recalada for a trip to Algeria at a better $11,500 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, the market has been under further pressure this week. A significant overhang of tonnage going into April leaves charterers in the driving seat and rates have eased accordingly with S-Oil covering trips to Onsan at both WS 45.5 and WS 45 for 274,000 and 270,000 tonne cargoes respectively, while 270,000 tonnes to China/Taiwan has been covered at WS 50 and a run to Thailand went at WS 52.5.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, the market has been in steady decline. A slow week saw enquiries receive a good response with 6/7 offers being registered each time and after starting the week at WS 97.5, rates eased down to WS 90 and have continued to fall, presently sitting at WS 85 for Europe discharge.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean has been the star performer this week as a surge of enquiry saw a clear out of tonnage with rates initially increasing by around 20 WS points. Rates rose to WS 127.5 for Black Sea loading and Petroineos reportedly paid WS 125 from Ceyhan.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to the US Gulf has been under renewed pressure. With panamax rates in the Caribbean sliding over 30 WS points, ballasters tend to focus more on the Continent/Transatlantic runs and rates today are around WS 115 for 55,000 tonnes to the US Gulf, representing a drop of around 10 points from last week.

title: Clean
summary: Rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC fell significantly. After starting the week around WS 185, Repsol covered a North Spain load at WS 160 as tonnage from West Med showed a willingness to compete here.

title: Capesize
summary: Still a largely depressing week for the big ships although there was an increase in rates from West Australia to China for late March but this largely the result of draft issues at Dampier prompting a premium. Rio Tinto conceded $4.70 for a 28 March onwards 170,000 tonne 10% cargo from Dampier to Qingdao and the charterer reportedly remained in the market.

title: Panamax
summary: South American activity drove the market this week with active fixing and improvement in rates for cargoes to the east. A 74,000 tonner 2000-built reportedly agreed $12,000 daily plus a $200,000 bonus for 9-14 April from east coast South America to the East.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Activity picked up in the US Gulf as the week drew to a close, earlier in the week a prompt 58,000 dwt went for a trip to Italy at $11,700 daily and latterly a 63,500 dwt ultramax secured $14,000 daily for a petcoke trip US Gulf to Italy. A number of front-haul trips from the Gulf have also been in evidence, including a Tess 52 fixing a trip with grain for mid-April to Japan at $11,500 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, charterers have largely held the upper hand. Rates dipped down to WS 48 to China and there was even one deal done at WS 45 but this is understood to have been on a ‘handicapped ship' with limited approvals so brokers feel this was not a true reflection of the market.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, the market firmed at the start of the week as rates rose from WS 82.5 to WS 87.5 and finally to a high of WS 90 as activity increased markedly. However, as charterers latterly held off, their tactics seem to have been successful as a trip to Canada went at WS 87.5 while a cargo for Europe enticed six offers and is also now reported to have gone on subjects at WS 87.5.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean had a frenetic start to the week with strong activity from Ceyhan and bad weather leading to a number of replacement cargoes. For non replacement business rates rose quickly to WS 140/145 as tonnage with a safe itinerary went at a premium.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from Continent to the US Gulf has been slow with rates struggling at around WS 110 for 55,000 tonnes. With a couple of ships left for first decade April, the immediate outlook is for status quo to be maintained.

title: Clean
summary: The market for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC has been very volatile this week. An initial fall to the low WS 150s saw more enquiry come to the fore which helped push rates back up WS 165, but then some ships failed on subjects and the market fell back again and presently sits at around WS 157.5.

title: Capesize
summary: Rates remained at very low levels across the market and any slight gains were just that with owners fighting over five to ten cents. The Atlantic saw more activity this week with finally some transatlantic activity with the Bolivar/Rotterdam for 150,000 to 160,000-tonne 10% cargo reaching $5.00 and some talk that more has been done.

title: Panamax
summary: South American grain shipments largely dominated the market this week with rates showing some improvements for trips to the East and transatlantic. Charterers were looking to take ships on a dop basis, with delays evident in Santos and Paranagua, although few delays evident in Argentina.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A slightly disappointing week in most areas after earlier optimism seemed to run out of steam. In the south Atlantic however, rates did appear to be at least steady as reports emerged of a 2006-built 55,600 dwt vessel being booked by a grain house for a trip from south Brazil to Algeria at about $11,000 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, there was an initial dip in the market as the Easter holidays took their toll - long East trips went at WS 48/48.5 level at the start of the week. However with a healthy level of enquiry as charterers started working third decade positions and a more balanced position list, the market turned around quickly with rates firstly increasing to WS 55 for China as Shell took the Apolytares and Vitol paid 57.5 basis Singapore discharge.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: Although West Africa has been busy this week with around 20 fixtures concluded in a short week, sheer volume of tonnage lead to charterers being able to squeeze owners and rates dropped from WS 75 at the end of last week down to WS 67.5 for European discharge while WS 65 was agreed for the US Gulf. Owners' cause is not being helped by a weaker market in the Middle East Gulf, meaning owners with tonnage east of Suez have been predominantly focusing on the West Africa market leading to more competition and placing the market under renewed pressure.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean has been under pressure this week with the Easter holidays leading to further build-up of tonnage here. Activity has largely been off market with charterers able to pick off suitable tonnage accordingly.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market from the Continent to the US Gulf has been steady with rates marginally firmer at WS 115 for 55,000 tonnes. A clear out of early tonnage, aided also by a firmer Caribbean Panamax market enticing more tonnage to stay local, has led to less supply of ballasters looking to play the Continent market.

title: Clean
summary: The market for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC has been steady this week with the market holding at WS 140. By contrast it has been a somewhat more volatile week on the 38,000 tonne backhaul route from the US Gulf to UK-Cont.

title: Capesize
summary: There was some upwards pressure for transatlantic rates and on the key Puerto Bolivar/Rotterdam coal run rates were being fixed around the $5.50 level. There was limited timecharter activity and fronthaul rates reported were still not much more than the low to mid $10,000 daily range.

title: Panamax
summary: South America has driven the market this week lending some support to the Atlantic and the East. Levels have improved on aps basis from east coast South America to the East with good kamsarmax rates hovering around the mid $12,000 daily range and $250,000 bonus.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A fairly uninspiring week for supramaxs with rates in most areas just about holding at ‘last done'. In the Atlantic there was a reasonable amount of fresh cargo however the supply of tonnage was sufficient to keep a lid on rates.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, the market has remained steady, with rates for Singapore basis 270,000 tonnes holding at WS 65 and long east at around WS 62.5. Going west, Bahri have been active and have paid both WS31 and also WS 33 cape/cape basis 280,000 tonnes to the US Gulf.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, an active week saw rates initially being maintained at WS 67.5, thereafter as more enquiry came in to the market, owners were able to push rates up gradually - Shell paid WS 68.75 and thereafter ‘Sikinos' agreed WS 72.5 for Saras from Angola to Italy. The arb has also opened for fuel going from UK-Cont-Baltic/going east, thereby taking away potential ballasters to West Africa which according to brokers seems to be firming.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean has been steady at around low WS 100s for Cross-med runs with rates being both voyage and date sensitive - a long voyage from Ceyhan to Fos was fixed at WS 102.5, while shorter runs from Ceyhan to Italy have subsequently been covered at both WS 105 and WS 107.5, while a short Algeria/Portugal trip went at WS 107.5. Black Sea levels dropped to WS 105 but then a replacement cargo off end April is understood to have been booked at WS 120.

title: Panamaxes
summary: After WS 115 from Continent to US Gulf for 55,000 tonnes was done, April tonnage has been thinned somewhat, leading to more bullish ideas from owners who are now understood to be aiming for WS 120 plus for this trade.

title: Clean
summary: It has been an uneventful week in the market for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC where rates have held steady at WS 140. On the 38,000 tonne backhaul route from US Gulf to UK Continent, it has been a week of two halves with the market firming modestly from high WS 80s up to WS 95 on the back of some prompt enquiry, as steady demand for central and South America initially took away tonnage.

title: Capesize
summary: Little change on the key routes with West Australia/China rates for a 170,000 tonne 10% cargo hovering around the mid $4.00 range for both Port Hedland and Dampier as draughts return to normal levels in the latter area. Timecharter rates have been in the doldrums although a well described 178,000 tonner open South Korea allegedly agreed $6,000 daily for a West Australian round.

title: Panamax
summary: South America remained the driving force absorbing tonnage from the East and from the Atlantic, with the East providing the lion's share. Rates for aps east coast South America to Singapore-Japan ranged from the upper $11,000 daily plus the upper $100,000 bonus to the $12,500 daily plus $250,000 bonus depending on the size and specification of the ship.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: In the Atlantic some areas were showing signs of life as more grain enquiry from the Black Sea region gave owners grounds for optimism with better rates being discussed. The South Atlantic seemed to be more or less unchanged as reports emerged of a 2010 56,000 dwt unit being fixed delivery Recalada for a trip to Skaw-Passero at $12,800 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: An active start to the week in the Middle East Gulf saw the market continue to firm as PTT took two ships both at WS 69 for discharge Thailand and Chevtex also agreed WS 69 for a Singapore run, all basis 270,000 cargo. Subsequently a lull in activity ensued as charterers worked on a more private basis in an effort to dent owners' bullish ideas and this tactic would appear to have been successful as rates have eased to WS 67 for Singapore and a cargo to Onsan went at WS 60 for 274,000.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, high levels of fixing for first decade May saw rates firm to WS 80 although a Cepsa re-let is understood midweek to have agreed WS 77.5 with Petrogal for a short trip to Portugal. Delta tonnage fixed and failed with ST at WS 82.5 but with a trip to EC Canada going at WS 78.75, the market to Europe is looking settled at WS 80.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean has been steady with rates holding at WS 100 for Cross-med runs. Early in the week there was a cheap fixture done at WS 87.5 from Sidi Kerir to Portugal, but this was on handicapped tonnage with limited approvals.

title: Panamaxes
summary: It has been a better week for owners here with WS 122.5 having now been done from Continent to US Gulf for 55,000, with owners now aiming to push up further and understood to be talking WS 125 plus.

title: Clean
summary: The market has remained steady for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC where rates have largely held at WS 140, although Statoil are reported to have fixed and failed at WS 145 if ARA load and WS 155 if Mongstad. However with a firmer backhaul rate in the US Gulf, tonnage is focussing more on ballasting down from USAC, than back across to the Continent.

title: Capesize
summary: An uneventful week for capesizes with rates largely flat and any gains in rates proving short lived as the market suffers from a surplus of tonnage. The West Australia/China rate moved in a very narrow range and closed the week around $4.40 for 170,000 tonner 10% cargoes from either Port Hedland or Dampier.

title: Panamax
summary: South American grain shipments have largely underpinned the market but trading here slowed as the week closed out and holidays globally are likely to slow much needed fresh inquiry. Rates had been holding steady but there was talk of a kamsarmax fixing an 11-16 May cargo from east coast South America to the east at $11,500 daily plus a $150,000 bonus.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: An unexciting week for the supramaxes as public holidays in various parts of the world inevitably had an effect. The only region within the Atlantic where owners managed to enjoy better fortunes was the Black Sea/east Mediterranean area.

title: VLCCs
summary: The market in the Middle East Gulf has been steady this week - levels for 270,000 tonnes have held at around WS 60 for long east while Singapore discharge has been covered at around WS 62/62.5. At the start of the week a low fixture was done at WS 49.5 for 274,000 tonnes to Onsan but this was for a ‘handicapped' ship on its maiden voyage, so would not be considered a true reflection of the market.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, it has been a slower week. Levels were initially holding at WS 80 for Europe discharge, but there is weaker sentiment in the market, borne out by Petrobras who are understood to have covered a short run to Brazil at WS 79 while US Gulf discharge has reportedly been fixed at WS 75.

title: Aframaxes
summary: There has been no ‘conference rate ‘ in the Mediterranean this week. Ceyhan has been steady at around ws110/112.5.

title: Panamaxes
summary: It has been an active week and with charterers now working up to 20 May position, owners have managed to achieve WS 125 from Continent to the US Gulf for 55,000 tonnes.

title: Clean
summary: An active week on the Continent has seen the tonnage list tighten and rates have firmed accordingly for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC. After being stuck in the low WS 140s, owners first managed to push rates to WS 150 and there is now a report of Exxon paying WS 165 for Port Jerome loading although there are restrictions here which limit the choice of workable tonnage.

title: Capesize
summary: Voyage rates improved for capesizes on the back of higher bunker prices. The majors were again active from West Australia to China and today saw rates reach $4.70 with a 160,000 tonne 10% cargo fixed for 20-22 May shipment from Port Hedland to Qingdao - up about 30 cents over the week.

title: Panamax
summary: A slowdown in South American activity undermined the market with much of the May business now absorbed but many May ships are still en route to the area. A 77,000 tonner 2012 built went to a major grain house for 20-30 May delivery east coast South America to the East at just $10,000 daily plus a $100,000 bonus.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Clinker business to West Africa together with more enquiry to the East led to a more active week in the east Mediterranean/Black Sea area. Rates accordingly started to show some improvement as reports emerged of a 2004 built 56,000 dwt vessel being booked delivery Nemrut Bay for a trip to Singapore-Japan at $9,000 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf this week it has been a two-tier market with ‘handicapped ships' being picked off in the low WS 50s. S-Oil took the Genmar Hercules at WS 50.5 basis 280,000 tonnes for Onsan discharge, but this ship has no sire or approvals after change of management.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, it has been a slower week. Levels were initially holding at WS 80 for Europe discharge, but there is weaker sentiment in the market, borne out by Petrobras who are understood to have covered a short run to Brazil at WS 79 while US Gulf discharge has reportedly been fixed at WS 75.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The Mediterranean has seen little change with rates holding steady at WS 102.5/105 level while Libya cargoes pay a premium of around 20 points. Delays and uncertainty regarding itineraries for tonnage discharging in Trieste have helped maintain the status quo here.

title: Panamaxes
summary: It has been a steady week with levels holding at around WS 122.5 having now been done from Continent to US Gulf for 55,000 tonnes, although there is potential for more tonnage to ballast across with Caribbean rates having eased below WS 130 for 50,000 tonnes for up coast discharge.

title: Clean
summary: A slow week has seen rates gradually ease from a high of WS 157.5 for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC to WS 155 and there is now a report of possibly WS 150 having been agreed here. Rates for 38,000 tonnes from the US Gulf have been steady throughout the week at WS 100, although the main activity here has again tended to see destinations of Central and South America absorbing the lion's share of the enquiry.

title: Capesize
summary: A combination of higher bunker prices and a drawdown of ore stocks in China spurred active fixing and this combined with a touch more activity in the Atlantic resulted in some significant gains albeit still at a low base. Midweek saw active trading, with Rio Tinto and BHP Billiton fixing and rates reaching at least $5.60.

title: Panamax
summary: Ships in the East saw some gains this week with a steady stream of new business and owners finally able in many instances to move away from aps and fix dop. Increased domestic China coal movements kept some Chinese ships off the market.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Little activity in the Atlantic as European holidays led to a flat market with very few reported fixtures. In the US Gulf a 2011 built 61,400 dwt vessel was reported to have been booked for a trip to Singapore-Japan at around $12,000 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: A very positive tone in all regions. In the Middle East Gulf rates firmed significantly as the week progressed, due to delays in Basrah and weather delays in the East reducing available tonnage.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, with tonnage tight, rates to the US Gulf moved up and Exxon fixed WS 85 on the Patroclus . Petrogal had to pay WS 135 for a cargo to Portugal basis 3 June loading.

title: Aframaxes
summary: Excess tonnage maintained the weaker tone and with Trieste up & running the charterers have pushed rates further down with WS 95 fixed basis Ceyhan and WS 90 being agreed by Socar on Sovcomflot tonnage for Black Sea loading. Maintenance at Primorsk due to last one week caused Baltic rates to drop to WS 70 level, before recovering back around WS 80.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market has held steady here throughout the week at around WS 122.5 for Continent to the US Gulf, for 55,000 tonnes.

title: Clean
summary: A see-saw week where rates dropped to low WS 140s, but as tonnage thinned rates climbed back up to WS 160 level. For 38,000mt from the US Gulf, rates have continued to increase on the back of strong enquiry, much of which has been for central and South America discharge.

title: Capesize
summary: What a difference a week can make, with last week's optimism waning. It seemed that the briefest pause in this market resulted in some jittery owners and operators conceding cents here and there.

title: Panamax
summary: Transatlantic trading was once again very slow with just a few short rounds reported fixed and a handful of coal cargoes on voyage basis showing very low returns. Short Baltic rounds were paying less than $6,000 daily while the US Gulf remained very slow, both transatlantic and fronthaul.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Another unexciting week within the Atlantic basin. In the US Gulf, a 2001 built 52,404 dwt ‘Tess 52' type was reportedly booked for a pet coke run to the east Mediterranean at a reasonable $11,500 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: For VLCC owners it has been another positive week in all areas. In the Middle East Gulf, short trips to Thailand have been covered at both WS 85 and subsequently WS 83, while long east trips have gone at between WS 71 and WS 75 all basis 270,000 tonnes.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, it has been a volatile market - end May/early June cargoes put charterers under pressure and Petrogal finally re-fixed at WS 130 while a short trip to South Africa went at WS 152.5. However, after ‘ the ‘tricky' positions were covered, rates for end first decade June have eased with WS 110 now agreed by Repsol for Spain discharge.

title: Aframaxes
summary: Having started the week in the high WS 90s, rates soared, with a high of WS 160 being agreed on subjects for a replacement cargo from Ceyhan for 28 May loading. Earlier ENI were reported to have agreed WS 137.5 for 2 June position, while Statoil off 29 May are understood to have paid WS 150, with the same level paid by Chevtex for very end May loading from Black Sea.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market has again held steady here throughout the week at around WS 122.5 from Continent to US Gulf for 55,000 tonnes. However with very limited tonnage availability and the aframax market strong making them uncompetitive, there is the potential for rates to firm here.

title: Clean
summary: It has been a good week for owners here with rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC gaining around WS 25 points to reach a peak of WS 190. However, with the fixing window moving in to early June and with a number of ships still available prior to then, there is now a softer feel to the market.

title: Capesize
summary: A short week due to the Spring Bank holiday ended in a flurry of fixtures for west Australia to China. Possibly over 10 vessels being concluded yesterday pushed the level from under $5.00 last week to $5.15.

title: Panamax
summary: The centre of attention this week has been front-haul activity from South America and with increased t/a enquiry from South America, the market looked to be holding steady. On the other hand, the north Continent remains weak with poor returns on offer.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: Some gains (albeit modest) were recorded on the US Gulf front-haul markets as reports surfaced of a nice 2014 built 61,000 dwt ultramax being fixed for a trip to China with petcoke at $13,350 daily. There was also talk as the week closed that a slightly better rate had been concluded on a similar vessel for a grain run to Japan.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, a lull in activity following the long weekend has led to the market coming under pressure. Rates here have dropped significantly with China discharge being fixed at WS 63.5 basis 270,000 tonnes on Delta Millenium , although there is a suggestion this vessel may be scheduled for dry dock in China.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates have continued to soften with the market from very low WS 100s a week ago down to WS 95 for Europe discharge, while P66 reportedly took Euronav tonnage to the US Gulf at WS 92.5 with USAC at WS 95. In the Black Sea, it has again been a slow week.

title: Aframaxes
summary: Despite the long weekend, the Mediterranean has held steady throughout the week with good levels of enquiry helping sustain levels here with both Med and Black Sea being covered at WS 137.5/140 level. A healthy tonnage list combined with a lack of enquiry has seen rates from the Baltic for 100,000 tonnes continue to soften with last done to UK-Cont being covered at WS 95, representing a drop of 12.5 points from a week ago.

title: Panamaxes
summary: With a stronger panamax market in the Caribbean enticing potential ballasters to stay local, the market for 55,000 tonnes from Continent to the US Gulf has again held steady with levels still around WS 122.5/125, with tonnage looking tight here for first half June.

title: Clean
summary: It has been a volatile week for owners here with rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC initially dropping down to WS 150 before regaining lost ground to WS 170 as healthy levels of enquiry thinned the tonnage list, with Baltic/UKCont enquiry to the fore here. Rates for 38,000 tonnes from the US Gulf have been steady throughout the week holding at WS 100 level, though again here, the enquiry has predominantly been for Central and South America discharge.

title: Capesize
summary: A largely flat week for capesizes with rates in the East moving in a narrow range on voyage basis. There were some improved numbers reported for timecharter but again the trading remained somewhat erratic.

title: Panamax
summary: South America remained the focus of activity with charterers paying firmer rates for June loaders. As rates dropped in recent weeks for cargo from east coast South America, some owners stopped ballasting helping to create this shortage.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A week of marking time for the supramax sector as the market continues to stumble along at mainly uninspiring levels, with the occasional pocket of resistance here and there. In the US Gulf, a 2004 built 55,600 dwt vessel was fixed when where ready Mississippi river for a trip to Singapore-Japan range at a steady $12,000 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: In the Middle East Gulf, the market softened further at the start of the week with rates for Singapore dipping down to around WS 63 and long east finding a new level of around WS 60/61 for 270,000 tonnes cargo. Deals have been done starting with a ‘5' but this has tended to be for ‘handicapped tonnage' which is either ex drydock or has no valid sire.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates to Europe for 130,000 tonnes initially dropped down to WS 87.5 before staging a small recovery with a high of WS 92.5 paid. Total were very active and confirmed 4 suezmaxes at between WS 89/90 in addition to the Athenian VLCC.

title: Aframaxes
summary: The start of the week, after a couple of deals failed, saw levels drop around 20 WS points to WS 120 - thereafter rates have held steady and with delays and uncertainty regarding prospects for tonnage in Trieste, brokers feel there is potential for rates to improve modestly. In the Baltic, rates have been volatile.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market for 55,000 tonnes from Continent to the US Gulf has again held steady. A Baltic/Transatlantic went at WS 130 at the start of the week and owners are understood to be pushing to improve on this level now.

title: Clean
summary: It has again been a volatile week for owners here with rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC initially easing to WS 150 before regaining lost ground to WS 160, aided by healthy levels of enquiry for short haul trips from the Baltic which have helped thin out tonnage here. We now understand that WS 157.5 is on subs with a slightly weaker sentiment again prevailing.

title: Capesize
summary: Early this week the market started with a slightly softer tone of minimal drops and has finished with only the Atlantic showing any slight improvement. The benchmark C3 Brazil/China fell almost 50 cents to a shade under $10.25 and on the C5 west Australia/China it has hovered around $4.95 level all week, a rate that was said to have been fixed on several vessels in the last 2 days by BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto & FMG.

title: Panamax
summary: Rates have improved significantly from last week with fewer ballasters available and additional cargoes needing to be covered. Tightness in South America has led to better levels for both Atlantic and Far East destinations, like the Silver Navigator 80,311 dwt built 2011 delivery passing Cape of Good Hope for a trip to the Far East at $8,500 + $275,000.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: In the Atlantic, significantly better rates were being seen from the US-Gulf area. A number of vessels were thought to be on subs or ‘closely working' as the week closed, but earlier in the week it was reported that a 2014 built 56,600 dwt ship had been fixed for a trip from the US Gulf to Finland at $12,000 daily.

title: VLCCs
summary: Short east to Singapore-Thailand has been covered at WS 63/64 level while long east has been going at around WS 60/61 level for 270,000 tonnes cargo. Adnatco failed on ore/oil carrier Olympic Lion at WS 56.5 and instead took Greek Warrior at WS 60.25 for Japan discharge, basis 265,000 tonnes cargo.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates to Europe for 130,000 tonnes have continued to drop and after starting the week in the high WS 80s, the market has settled here at WS 80. However, for USAC discharge Suncor covered on SCF Altai at an aggressive WS 72.5.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean it has been a very active and firmer week due to renewed enquiry from Libya, delays in Trieste and replacement business. Rates rose from WS 125 at the start of the week to WS 142.5, achieved by Arcadia tonnage for a Ceyhan/Med trip.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market for 55,000 tonnes from Continent to US Gulf remains unchanged at WS 127.5 as steady levels of enquiry have helped absorb the tonnage.

title: Clean
summary: It has been a week of steady, if relatively modest gains, with rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC up around 10 points. WS 162.5 was confirmed and WS 165 has fixed/failed twice.

title: Capesize
summary: An upbeat week generally for the big ships but there remained a fragility about the market that even with rates rising, some became increasingly nervous about how long it would last. The West Australia/China rate certainly reached $5.75 but it was never established whether $6.00 was agreed.

title: Panamax
summary: South American activity has largely shaped activity generally. As charterers piled in to take tonnage absorbing ballasters from the East and ships from the North Atlantic, rates rose quickly.

title: Supramax / Handysize
summary: A more encouraging week for supramaxes in most areas. In the Atlantic the US Gulf markets continued to push and although the week ended on a quiet note, rates being discussed were still thought to be relatively firm.

title: VLCCs
summary: In all areas the market has been firm. In the Middle East Gulf a Japanese replacement cargo was the catalyst for the strengthening market with WS 67 paid for Japan discharge.

title: Suezmaxes
summary: In West Africa, rates to Europe for 130,000 tonnes started the week at WS 80. Thereafter rates have been on a steady climb with WS 100 now having been paid as a combination of ullage delays in the East for suezmaxes with fuel oil onboard, together with ships in the Atlantic still awaiting discharge orders for unsold cargoes, have significantly reduced the available ballasters back for West Africa loading.

title: Aframaxes
summary: In the Mediterranean, rates have been steady with levels holding in the mid WS 130 from both East Med and Black Sea with Libya cargoes paying around 10/15 points premium. In the Baltic, rates have again been volatile.

title: Panamaxes
summary: The market for 55,000 tonnes from Continent to the US Gulf has firmed here also with a Baltic/Transatlantic cargo being fixed at WS 130 and subsequently owners have been aiming for WS 135 as ballasters from USA have looked to stay local on the back of a firmer up coast market affected by weather delays.

title: Clean
summary:
Rates for 37,000 tonnes from Continent to USAC firmed in the first half of the week with WS 192.5 being the high for the week before easing back to WS 180 while levels for 38,000 tonnes from the US Gulf to UK-Cont were in the low/mid WS 120s at the start of the week before easing around five points, but owners have now regained lost ground to again sit at WS 125 level.
